tagline: Think like an attacker. Defend like a professional.
blurb: IL-25 is a 96-hour independent practice course aligned to the public topic map of a well-known 24-week professional cybersecurity certificate program. Across three phases — risk and governance foundations, defensive operations, and offensive security plus capstone — you build firewalls, triage logs, dissect phishing, audit cloud configurations, scope pentests, and close with a portfolio-grade capstone and a 120-minute mock circuit.

objectives: Assess organizational cyber risk using the threat-vulnerability-impact model and communicate findings in business terms.
Design layered defensive architectures spanning network, endpoint, identity, and data controls aligned to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework.
Execute incident response operations following the NIST SP 800-61 lifecycle, from detection through post-incident lessons learned.
Analyze adversarial techniques using MITRE ATT&CK and the cyber kill chain to build detections and prioritize defenses.
Evaluate cloud, OT/IoT, and AI systems for misconfigurations and emerging threats, applying appropriate guardrails.
Construct professional security deliverables — risk registers, pentest reports, and IR timelines — suitable for a hiring portfolio.

arc.title: Risk & Governance Foundations
arc.body: Modules 1-8 build the bedrock: risk management and the CIA triad, computing and networking foundations, federal law and standards (NIST CSF, RMF), threats and vulnerabilities, critical infrastructure, identity and access management, defensive operations concepts, and cryptography. You learn to speak risk, read the law and frameworks, and understand how systems are attacked and defended at a structural level.

arc.title: Defensive Operations
arc.body: Modules 9-16 put you in the defender's seat: SOC operations and SIEM-driven detection, incident response per NIST SP 800-61, secure system and network administration, cloud security and the shared responsibility model, then the adversary's view through offensive security concepts, social engineering, and AI security. Every module pairs theory with hands-on labs — firewall rules, log triage, header analysis, IAM audits.

arc.title: Offensive Security & Capstone
arc.body: Modules 17-24 complete the arc: penetration testing methodology with strict scoping and rules of engagement, policy/privacy/governance, OT/IoT security, and a capstone project where you run a full engagement lifecycle — threat model, defend, detect, respond, and report. You graduate with a portfolio artifact and a 120-minute mock circuit proving readiness.

battlePlan.title: Risk & Foundations Sprint
battlePlan.detail: Modules 1-2: risk equation and treatment, CIA triad, OSI/TCP-IP, lab on password entropy. Deliverable: a one-page risk register for a fictional small business.

battlePlan.detail: Modules 3-5: NIST CSF 2.0 functions, federal law basics, threat/vuln taxonomy, MITRE ATT&CK intro, CISA sectors. Deliverable: map five ATT&CK techniques to CSF functions.

battlePlan.title: IAM & Defensive Ops Sprint
battlePlan.detail: Modules 6-7: least privilege, MFA, RBAC, default-deny firewalls, IDS/IPS/SIEM. Labs: iptables rule build, IAM policy audit. Deliverable: hardened host firewall script.

battlePlan.title: Cryptography & SOC Sprint
battlePlan.detail: Modules 8-9: symmetric/asymmetric crypto, hashing vs encryption, TLS checks, SOC tiers and alert triage. Labs: hash identification, SOC triage runbook. Deliverable: triage checklist.

battlePlan.title: IR & Secure Administration Sprint
battlePlan.detail: Modules 10-11: NIST SP 800-61 lifecycle, evidence handling, log triage, server hardening, patching. Labs: auth-log triage, IR timeline builder. Deliverable: incident timeline from sample logs.

battlePlan.title: Cloud & Offensive Concepts Sprint
battlePlan.detail: Modules 12-13: shared responsibility, misconfiguration audit, black/white/gray-box testing, kill chain. Lab: cloud misconfiguration audit. Deliverable: audit findings memo.

handsOnLab.title: Hands-on lab: Introduction to Cybersecurity Risk Management
handsOnLab.brief: You will perform a structured risk analysis on a realistic scenario using this module's concepts: identify threats and vulnerabilities, rank risks qualitatively, select treatments, and write it up as a professional findings memo. The deliverable is the memo — the core work product of security practice.
steps: Write a one-paragraph scenario: a small organization, its key assets, and its threat context (Define threat, vulnerability, impact, likelihood, and residual risk in plain language.). Keep it realistic and specific.
Identify five threat–vulnerability pairs. For each, state the threat actor/capability, the vulnerability, and the impact in plain language.
Rank the five risks qualitatively (threat × vulnerability × impact) into high/medium/low. Justify each ranking in one sentence — no false precision with made-up numbers.
For each risk, choose a treatment: avoid, mitigate, transfer, or accept — with the concrete control or decision for each. Note residual risk explicitly.
Write the findings memo: executive summary (5 lines), risk register table, recommended treatments with owners, and residual risks requiring sign-off.
Re-read the memo as the executive: is every recommendation actionable, and is the residual risk stated honestly? Revise until yes.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Risk** — the potential for loss or harm when a threat exploits a vulnerability; commonly expressed as threat × vulnerability × impact.
- **Threat** — anything that could cause harm: a ransomware gang, a phishing email, a disgruntled employee, or a flood.
- **Vulnerability** — a weakness a threat can exploit: an unpatched server, a weak password policy, or an unlocked door.
- **Impact** — the damage if the event happens: money lost, downtime, reputational harm, legal penalties.
- **Likelihood** — how probable the event is, estimated from history, threat intelligence, and exposure.
- **Risk treatments** — avoid (stop the activity), mitigate (add controls), transfer (buy cyber insurance), accept (document and live with it).
- **Residual risk** — the risk left over after controls are applied; it is what leadership formally accepts.
- **Risk appetite** — how much risk an organization will take to achieve its goals; it guides every prioritization call.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Open a blank spreadsheet and create columns: Asset, Threat, Vulnerability, Likelihood (1–5), Impact (1–5), Risk score, Treatment, Owner.
1. List five assets you care about: your laptop, your email account, a family photo archive, your home router, and one work or school account.
2. For each asset, write one realistic threat and the vulnerability it would exploit (e.g., threat: credential-stuffing bots; vulnerability: password reuse).
3. Score likelihood and impact 1–5 and multiply for a risk score.
4. Sort by score and assign each row a treatment — avoid, mitigate, transfer, or accept — plus a named owner (you).
5. Take the top row and write one concrete mitigation you can finish this week, such as enabling MFA or applying updates.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Write a one-page risk assessment memo for a fictional 20-person accounting firm. Identify its five most important information assets, list two threats per asset with the vulnerabilities each exploits, and score likelihood × impact. Recommend one treatment per top-three risk with a rough cost estimate (free, cheap, expensive). Close with the residual risk statement the firm's owner would sign. Deliverable: a single PDF or markdown page, plain language, no unexplained jargon.

Which of your own digital assets would hurt most to lose — and which treatment have you actually been applying to it: mitigation, or silent acceptance? Self-check: 1) What is the difference between a threat and a vulnerability? 2) Name the four risk treatments. 3) What is residual risk?

notes.title: Common mistakes: Introduction to Cybersecurity Risk Management
notes.body:
**Where cybersecurity learners go wrong — and the professional corrections.**

- **Tool-first thinking.** Knowing a scanner's buttons without understanding what the finding *means* produces noise, not security. Learn the underlying concept (e.g., what a vulnerability actually is) before the tool.
- **Checklist compliance mindset.** Controls exist to reduce risk, not to fill spreadsheets. Always ask: what threat does this control actually mitigate?
- **Ignoring the human layer.** Most breaches involve human factors; a purely technical view misses phishing, misconfiguration, and process failures.
- **Absolute language.** 'Unhackable', '100% secure', 'zero risk' — none of these exist. Security is risk management under uncertainty; speak in likelihoods and trade-offs.
- **No documentation habit.** Undocumented findings and actions are un-auditable. Write as if someone else must act on your notes at 3 AM.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Confidentiality** — information is accessible only to those authorized; enforced with encryption, access controls, and classification.
- **Integrity** — data is accurate and unaltered; protected with hashing, checksums, digital signatures, and change control.
- **Availability** — systems and data are reachable when needed; supported by redundancy, backups, and incident response.
- **Defense in depth** — layered controls (firewall, MFA, encryption, monitoring) so one failure does not equal total compromise.
- **Least privilege** — every user and process gets only the minimum access needed, shrinking the blast radius of compromise.
- **Zero trust** — “never trust, always verify”: verify every request, whatever the network location.
- **Attack surface** — the sum of all points where an attacker could get in: open ports, web apps, user accounts, APIs.
- **Authentication factors** — something you know (password), something you have (phone/token), something you are (fingerprint).

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run a personal security-basics audit.
1. List your ten most important online accounts (email, banking, school, work).
2. For each, record: does it use a unique password? Is MFA enabled? What factor type is the second factor?
3. Turn on MFA everywhere it is offered, preferring authenticator apps or passkeys over SMS.
4. Open your phone's app permissions and revoke location, camera, and contacts access from apps that do not need them — a least-privilege exercise.
5. Write a three-line summary: which account was your weakest link, and what did you change?

Then list three ways its attack surface could be reduced. Deliverable: a one-page write-up in plain language.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF)** — a voluntary, widely adopted framework organized into six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
- **Govern** — strategy, policy, and oversight: the organization's risk strategy and roles.
- **Identify** — know what you have: asset management, risk assessment, threat awareness.
- **Protect** — safeguards: access control, training, data security, hardening.
- **Detect** — monitoring and anomaly detection to catch events quickly.
- **Respond** — incident response planning, communications, and mitigation.
- **Recover** — restoring operations: backups, recovery planning, lessons learned.
- **FISMA** — requires federal agencies to implement information security protections and report on them.
- **CISA** — the federal operational lead for critical infrastructure protection and incident response coordination.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Do a mini CSF mapping exercise.
1. Pick an organization you know (a school, a small business, your home network).
2. Write down six real safeguards it already has — e.g., antivirus, backups, a firewall, password rules, software updates, an incident contact list.
3. Assign each safeguard to exactly one CSF function: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, or Recover.
4. Note which functions have zero safeguards — those are your gaps.
5. Draft one sentence per gap describing the cheapest realistic fix, and order the fixes by impact.

Include a simple table mapping five controls from your own environment to functions. Deliverable: a polished PDF or markdown document suitable for a board packet.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body: Compliance is a floor, not a ceiling — frameworks guide, but attackers don't read them. Ask yourself: which CSF function is weakest in your own setup? Self-check: 1) Name the six CSF functions in order. 2) What does FISMA require? 3) What is CISA's role?

notes.title: Common mistakes: The Federal Government Role: Law, Operations, and Stan…
notes.body:
**Where cybersecurity learners go wrong — and the professional corrections.**

- **Tool-first thinking.** Knowing a scanner's buttons without understanding what the finding *means* produces noise, not security. Learn the underlying concept (e.g., what a vulnerability actually is) before the tool.
- **Checklist compliance mindset.** Controls exist to reduce risk, not to fill spreadsheets. Always ask: what threat does this control actually mitigate?
- **Ignoring the human layer.** Most breaches involve human factors; a purely technical view misses phishing, misconfiguration, and process failures.
- **Absolute language.** 'Unhackable', '100% secure', 'zero risk' — none of these exist. Security is risk management under uncertainty; speak in likelihoods and trade-offs.
- **No documentation habit.** Undocumented findings and actions are un-auditable. Write as if someone else must act on your notes at 3 AM.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Malware** — malicious software: viruses need a host and user action; worms self-propagate; trojans pose as legitimate apps.
- **Ransomware** — encrypts data and demands payment for the key; often paired with data theft (double extortion).
- **Spyware** — secretly monitors activity and steals keystrokes and credentials.
- **Phishing** — fake messages impersonating trusted senders to steal credentials or deliver malware; spear phishing targets specific people.
- **Social engineering** — manipulating people, not systems: pretexting, baiting, and tailgating exploit trust and urgency.
- **Threat actors** — from lone criminals to ransomware gangs, hacktivists, insiders, and APTs.
- **CVE** — Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: the public catalog assigning unique IDs and severity scores to known vulnerabilities.
- **Scanning vs. pen testing** — scanning automatically finds known weaknesses; pen testers actively attempt exploitation under defined rules.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Practice safe reconnaissance on your own network.
1. Install Nmap (or use your package manager) on a machine you own.
2. Scan only your home network: `nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24` (adjust to your subnet) to list live hosts — never scan networks you do not own or have permission to test.
3. Pick one of your own devices and run a basic port scan: `nmap <its IP>`.
4. For each open port, note the likely service and ask: does this need to be exposed?
5. Look up one CVE for a service you found and read what the entry discloses: affected versions, impact, and fix.

- **IT vs. OT** — IT guards data confidentiality; OT guards the safety and availability of physical processes, often on aging gear.
- **SCADA** — Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition: operators monitor and control industrial processes through sensor data.
- **ICS** — industrial control systems: SCADA plus programmable logic controllers (PLCs).
- **IT/OT convergence** — linking control networks to business networks and the internet: efficient, but it exposes OT to IT-style attacks.
- **Resilience** — keeping essential services running, or restoring them fast, during and after an incident.
- **Safety instrumented systems** — last-resort safeguards that shut a process down safely when controls fail.

notes.body:

1. Write a one-paragraph scenario: ransomware has encrypted the billing network and is probing the SCADA network.

notes.title: Common mistakes: Cybersecurity for Critical Urban Infrastructure
notes.body:
**Where cybersecurity learners go wrong — and the professional corrections.**

- **Tool-first thinking.** Knowing a scanner's buttons without understanding what the finding *means* produces noise, not security. Learn the underlying concept (e.g., what a vulnerability actually is) before the tool.
- **Checklist compliance mindset.** Controls exist to reduce risk, not to fill spreadsheets. Always ask: what threat does this control actually mitigate?
- **Ignoring the human layer.** Most breaches involve human factors; a purely technical view misses phishing, misconfiguration, and process failures.
- **Absolute language.** 'Unhackable', '100% secure', 'zero risk' — none of these exist. Security is risk management under uncertainty; speak in likelihoods and trade-offs.
- **No documentation habit.** Undocumented findings and actions are un-auditable. Write as if someone else must act on your notes at 3 AM.

modules.title: Identity and Access Management (IAM) Concepts
modules.summary: Identity is the new perimeter: most breaches start with a stolen or misused credential. This module covers authentication, authorization, and the account lifecycle — the IAM concepts behind every login screen you will ever defend. Independent study aligned to the MIT xPRO Professional Certificate in Cybersecurity topic map; not affiliated with MIT and confers no certificate.
objectives: Distinguish authentication, authorization, and accounting (AAA).
Compare RBAC and ABAC access models.
Explain SSO, MFA, and passkeys and when each fits.
Describe the joiner-mover-leaver account lifecycle.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **AAA** — authentication proves who you are; authorization sets what you may do; accounting logs what you did.
- **MFA** — multi-factor authentication combines two or more factor types, blocking most credential attacks even when passwords leak.
- **Passkeys** — phishing-resistant, public-key credentials that replace passwords with device-bound key pairs.
- **SSO** — single sign-on: one login grants access to many apps, cutting password sprawl (but the identity provider becomes a prime target).
- **RBAC** — role-based access control: permissions attach to roles, and users inherit their role's permissions.
- **ABAC** — attribute-based access control: decisions weigh attributes like department, clearance, or time of day.
- **Least privilege** — accounts, especially privileged ones, hold only the access their role requires, reviewed regularly.
- **Joiner-mover-leaver** — the account lifecycle: provision on hire, adjust on role change, deprovision on departure.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Audit your own identity footprint.
1. Open your email account's security page and list every active session and connected third-party app.
2. Revoke sessions and app permissions you do not recognize or no longer use.
3. Enable MFA on the account using an authenticator app or passkey if supported.
4. Check whether your password appears in known breach data using a reputable breach-check service, and change it if exposed.
5. Write down your personal “leaver checklist”: the accounts you would lock down first if a device were stolen.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Identification** — the claim of who you are: a username, an account ID, a certificate subject. A claim alone carries no trust.
- **Authentication** — proving the claim with factors: something you know (password), something you have (hardware key), something you are (biometric). MFA requires two or more *different* factors; two passwords is not MFA.
- **Authorization** — what the proven identity may do. RBAC grants permissions through roles; ABAC evaluates attributes (department, device health, time). Both follow least privilege: only what the task needs.
- **Accountability** — binding actions to identities through logs so every grant, denial, and elevation is auditable.
- **Federation** — one identity provider vouches for users across services: SAML for enterprise SSO, OAuth 2.0 for delegated authorization, OpenID Connect for identity on top of OAuth.
- **Privileged access** — admin accounts get vaulted credentials, just-in-time elevation, and recorded sessions.

notes.title: Common mistakes: Preparing for a Job in Cybersecurity Risk Management
notes.body:
**Where cybersecurity learners go wrong — and the professional corrections.**

- **Tool-first thinking.** Knowing a scanner's buttons without understanding what the finding *means* produces noise, not security. Learn the underlying concept (e.g., what a vulnerability actually is) before the tool.
- **Checklist compliance mindset.** Controls exist to reduce risk, not to fill spreadsheets. Always ask: what threat does this control actually mitigate?
- **Ignoring the human layer.** Most breaches involve human factors; a purely technical view misses phishing, misconfiguration, and process failures.
- **Absolute language.** 'Unhackable', '100% secure', 'zero risk' — none of these exist. Security is risk management under uncertainty; speak in likelihoods and trade-offs.
- **No documentation habit.** Undocumented findings and actions are un-auditable. Write as if someone else must act on your notes at 3 AM.

- **Defense in depth** — layered controls so one failure is not total failure: perimeter, network segmentation, endpoint, application, data, people.

modules.title: Cryptography
modules.summary: Cryptography is the math that lets strangers trust each other over hostile networks. This module covers symmetric and asymmetric encryption, hashing, digital signatures, and PKI — what each one guarantees, what it does not, and where you meet them in everyday systems like TLS.
objectives: Distinguish symmetric from asymmetric encryption and choose the right one for a scenario
Explain what hashing guarantees and why it is not encryption
Describe how digital signatures provide authentication, integrity, and non-repudiation
Trace how PKI and certificates make TLS trust work in a browser session

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Symmetric encryption** — one shared secret key encrypts and decrypts (AES is the modern standard). Fast, suited to bulk data — but both sides must share the key securely first.
- **Asymmetric encryption** — key pair: public key encrypts, private key decrypts (RSA is the classic example). Solves key distribution but is slow, so it typically protects a symmetric session key.
- **Hashing** — a one-way function (SHA-256) producing a fixed-size digest. Not encryption: no key, no decryption. Used for integrity checks and password verifiers.
- **Digital signatures** — sign with the private key, verify with the public key: authentication, integrity, and non-repudiation.
- **Key exchange** — Diffie-Hellman lets two parties agree on a shared secret over a public channel, with no authentication by itself.
- **PKI and TLS** — certificate authorities vouch for public keys; browsers trust a preinstalled root list, which is what the padlock rests on.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body: Use OpenSSL on a lab machine to touch every primitive. 1) Generate an RSA key pair and a self-signed certificate. 2) Encrypt a short text file with the public key, then decrypt with the private key. 3) Hash the file with SHA-256, change one byte, and hash again to see the digest change completely. 4) Sign the file with the private key and verify the signature with the public key, then tamper the file and watch verification fail. 5) Write two sentences for each step: what security property did you just demonstrate?

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Write a one-page encryption design brief for a fictional clinic's patient portal. Specify: what gets symmetric encryption (AES for data at rest and the TLS session), where asymmetric crypto appears (key exchange, certificate-based server authentication), what gets hashed (password verifiers with a salt, file integrity checks), and where digital signatures are used (software updates, audit logs). Add a 'what it does not protect' section — e.g., encryption does not stop phishing or a compromised endpoint. Deliverable: the brief as a PDF.

**Problem.** AES is best described as:
A. A symmetric encryption algorithm used for bulk data ←
B. An asymmetric algorithm for digital signatures
C. A hashing function for password storage
D. A key-exchange protocol

**Walkthrough.**
1. Restate the question in your own words: it is asking about Cryptography — anchor every choice to the Concepts note, not to gut feel.
2. Eliminate the distractors: B (An asymmetric algorithm for digital signatures); C (A hashing function for password storage); D (A key-exchange protocol) — each contradicts the module's definitions (check the Concepts note line by line).
3. Confirm the survivor: A. AES uses one shared key for encryption and decryption and is the standard for bulk symmetric encryption. (Concepts)

notes.title: Common mistakes: Cryptography
notes.body:
**Where cybersecurity learners go wrong — and the professional corrections.**

- **Tool-first thinking.** Knowing a scanner's buttons without understanding what the finding *means* produces noise, not security. Learn the underlying concept (e.g., what a vulnerability actually is) before the tool.
- **Checklist compliance mindset.** Controls exist to reduce risk, not to fill spreadsheets. Always ask: what threat does this control actually mitigate?
- **Ignoring the human layer.** Most breaches involve human factors; a purely technical view misses phishing, misconfiguration, and process failures.
- **Absolute language.** 'Unhackable', '100% secure', 'zero risk' — none of these exist. Security is risk management under uncertainty; speak in likelihoods and trade-offs.
- **No documentation habit.** Undocumented findings and actions are un-auditable. Write as if someone else must act on your notes at 3 AM.

For *Cryptography*, tie every concept in Distinguish symmetric from asymmetric encryption and choose the right one for a scenario; Explain what hashing guarantees and why it is not encryption to a concrete threat and a concrete control — abstraction without application doesn't survive contact with real incidents.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **SOC tiers** — L1 triages alerts: acknowledge, enrich, escalate or close. L2 investigates confirmed incidents: scope, contain, coordinate. L3 hunts proactively, tunes detections, handles threat intelligence.
- **SIEM** — aggregates logs across the estate, correlates events into alerts, and gives analysts one searchable timeline. Only as good as its log sources and tuned rules.
- **Alert triage** — verify before acting: check raw logs, enrich with context (asset criticality, user role), rule true vs false positive, escalate with evidence attached.
- **Runbooks and playbooks** — step-by-step procedures for common alert types (phishing, malware, impossible travel) so L1 responds consistently at 3 AM.
- **Metrics** — MTTD (mean time to detect), MTTR (mean time to respond/recover), alert volume per analyst, false-positive rate. A drowning L1 queue signals bad tuning or understaffing.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body: Triage like an L1 analyst using sample data. 1) Take five mock alerts (impossible-travel login, malware hash match, port scan, failed logins x50, odd PowerShell). 2) For each, write: the raw evidence you would pull first, two enrichment questions (who owns the asset? is the user traveling?), and your disposition (true positive, false positive, benign, escalate). 3) Draft a three-line escalation note for the one you escalate to L2. 4) Finally, write one SIEM correlation rule in plain English that would have caught your true positive earlier. Time yourself: triage is a timed discipline.

modules.summary: When prevention fails, disciplined response limits the damage. This module teaches the NIST SP 800-61 incident response lifecycle — Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication, and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity — plus the evidence handling and communication habits that separate professionals from panickers.
objectives: Name and order the four NIST SP 800-61 incident response phases
Explain containment, eradication, and recovery as distinct steps with different goals
Describe evidence preservation and chain of custody during an incident
Run a tabletop exercise and write a lessons-learned report

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Phase 1: Preparation** — before anything happens: IR plan, defined roles, contact lists, tooling, trained staff, practiced playbooks. Not improvisable mid-incident.
- **Phase 2: Detection & Analysis** — validate the incident: confirm scope, determine what happened, prioritize by impact. Hasty conclusions cause wrong containment.
- **Phase 3: Containment, Eradication & Recovery** — containment stops the bleeding (isolate hosts, block indicators); eradication removes the cause (kill persistence, patch entry); recovery restores operations with heightened monitoring.
- **Phase 4: Post-Incident Activity** — lessons-learned review: timeline, what worked, what failed, improvements fed back into preparation.
- **Evidence handling** — preserve logs and images before remediation destroys them; keep chain of custody (who handled what, when).
- **Communication** — one spokesperson, need-to-know updates, prewritten templates.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body: Run a 45-minute tabletop exercise with a partner (or solo, writing both sides). Scenario: ransomware found on two finance workstations at 9 AM. 1) Preparation check: list the roles, contacts, and tools you would need — note what is missing. 2) Detection & Analysis: write the five questions you must answer before containing (patient zero? spread? data exfiltration?). 3) Containment/Eradication/Recovery: sequence your actions and justify the order. 4) Draft the internal notification for staff and the executive update. 5) Hold the lessons-learned: three things to improve. Keep the whole exercise to two pages.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Produce a two-page incident response plan for a fictional 40-person company plus a one-page lessons-learned template. The plan must cover: IR team roles and escalation contacts, the four NIST phases with entry/exit criteria for each, evidence-preservation steps, and communication rules (who speaks, who is told what, when legal is looped in). The template must capture timeline, root cause, impact, response effectiveness, and action items with owners. Deliverable: plan plus template as a single PDF.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body: Reflect: think of a past crisis (tech or otherwise) — what would a 'post-incident review' have caught that the moment itself missed? Self-check: 1) List the four NIST IR phases in order. 2) Why contain before eradicating? 3) What is chain of custody and why does it matter?

notes.title: Worked example: Incident Response (IR)
notes.body:
**Problem.** The correct order of the NIST SP 800-61 phases is:
A. Detection & Analysis; Preparation; Post-Incident Activity; Containment, Eradication & Recovery
B. Preparation; Containment, Eradication & Recovery; Detection & Analysis; Post-Incident Activity
C. Preparation; Detection & Analysis; Containment, Eradication & Recovery; Post-Incident Activity ←
D. Containment, Eradication & Recovery; Preparation; Detection & Analysis; Post-Incident Activity

**Walkthrough.**
1. Restate the question in your own words: it is asking about Incident Response (IR) — anchor every choice to the Concepts note, not to gut feel.
2. Eliminate the distractors: A (Detection & Analysis; Preparation; Post-Incident Activity;…); B (Preparation; Containment, Eradication & Recovery; Detection…); D (Containment, Eradication & Recovery; Preparation; Detection…) — each contradicts the module's definitions (check the Concepts note line by line).
3. Confirm the survivor: C. NIST SP 800-61 orders them: prepare, detect/analyze, contain/eradicate/recover, then learn. (Concepts)

**Solution.** C — Preparation; Detection & Analysis; Containment, Eradication & Recovery; Post-Incident Activity

*Try it yourself:* cover the solution, re-answer from memory, then check. If you missed it, re-read the Concepts note before moving on.

notes.title: Common mistakes: Incident Response (IR)
notes.body:
**Where cybersecurity learners go wrong — and the professional corrections.**

- **Tool-first thinking.** Knowing a scanner's buttons without understanding what the finding *means* produces noise, not security. Learn the underlying concept (e.g., what a vulnerability actually is) before the tool.
- **Checklist compliance mindset.** Controls exist to reduce risk, not to fill spreadsheets. Always ask: what threat does this control actually mitigate?
- **Ignoring the human layer.** Most breaches involve human factors; a purely technical view misses phishing, misconfiguration, and process failures.
- **Absolute language.** 'Unhackable', '100% secure', 'zero risk' — none of these exist. Security is risk management under uncertainty; speak in likelihoods and trade-offs.
- **No documentation habit.** Undocumented findings and actions are un-auditable. Write as if someone else must act on your notes at 3 AM.

For *Incident Response (IR)*, tie every concept in Name and order the four NIST SP 800-61 incident response phases; Explain containment, eradication, and recovery as distinct steps with different goals to a concrete threat and a concrete control — abstraction without application doesn't survive contact with real incidents.

handsOnLab.title: Hands-on lab: Incident Response (IR)
handsOnLab.brief: You will perform a structured risk analysis on a realistic scenario using this module's concepts: identify threats and vulnerabilities, rank risks qualitatively, select treatments, and write it up as a professional findings memo. The deliverable is the memo — the core work product of security practice.
steps: Write a one-paragraph scenario: a small organization, its key assets, and its threat context (Name and order the four NIST SP 800-61 incident response phases). Keep it realistic and specific.
Identify five threat–vulnerability pairs. For each, state the threat actor/capability, the vulnerability, and the impact in plain language.
Rank the five risks qualitatively (threat × vulnerability × impact) into high/medium/low. Justify each ranking in one sentence — no false precision with made-up numbers.
For each risk, choose a treatment: avoid, mitigate, transfer, or accept — with the concrete control or decision for each. Note residual risk explicitly.
Write the findings memo: executive summary (5 lines), risk register table, recommended treatments with owners, and residual risks requiring sign-off.
Re-read the memo as the executive: is every recommendation actionable, and is the residual risk stated honestly? Revise until yes.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A professional findings memo: executive summary, 5-row risk register with qualitative rankings and justifications, treatments with owners, and explicit residual risk.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Five threat–vulnerability pairs with plain-language impacts; rankings justified qualitatively; every treatment has an owner; residual risk explicitly stated.

choices: Preparation first, then Detection and Analysis, then Containment/Eradication/Recovery, then Post-Incident Activity: the NIST SP 800-61 order.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Hardening** — reducing a system’s attack surface by removing unneeded services, software, and accounts, then securing what remains.
- **Least privilege** — every user, process, and service receives only the permissions required for its job, nothing more.
- **CIS Benchmarks** — community-developed, vendor-neutral configuration baselines; a standard hardening starting point.
- **Patch management** — the cycle of inventorying assets, testing updates, deploying on schedule, and verifying; unpatched software is a top initial-access vector.
- **Secure baselines** — hardened images or configuration templates so every new host starts from a known-good state.
- **Account hygiene** — disable default accounts, enforce strong unique passwords plus MFA, and use separate privileged accounts for admin work.
- **Centralized logging** — forward authentication and privilege-escalation events to a collector; without logs you cannot detect or reconstruct incidents.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
1. On a lab Linux VM, update all packages and reboot.
2. List enabled services and disable anything non-essential.
3. Audit users: lock or remove unused accounts and verify there are no duplicate privileged UIDs.
4. Harden SSH: disable password authentication, require key-based login, and disable remote root login.
5. Enable the host firewall with a default-deny inbound policy, allowing only SSH from your management host.
6. From a second VM, run Nmap against the target and confirm only the expected port is open.
7. Document every change plus the before/after scan results in your lab notebook.

Deliver a 2–3 page report: checklist, before/after tables, residual risks, and a rollback note for each change.

Intrusion detection system: monitors traffic and raises alerts on malicious activity, but does not block it.
Intrusion prevention system: sits inline in the traffic path and can actively block malicious activity.
Virtual private network: an encrypted tunnel carrying private traffic across an untrusted network.
A switch feature that filters DHCP messages to block rogue DHCP servers and reduce spoofing attacks.
the rule set ends with a deny-all; only explicitly permitted traffic passes. Default-allow is never acceptable on a security boundary.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Default-deny firewalling** — the rule set ends with a deny-all; only explicitly permitted traffic passes. Default-allow is never acceptable on a security boundary.
- **Segmentation** — dividing the network into zones (VLANs, subnets) so a breach in one zone cannot freely reach the others; the main control against lateral movement.
- **DMZ** — a screened subnet for internet-facing services, isolated from both the internet and the internal network.
- **IDS vs IPS** — an intrusion *detection* system flags malicious traffic; an intrusion *prevention* system sits inline and can block it.
- **VPN** — encrypted tunnels for remote access and site-to-site links; authenticate users with MFA and restrict access by role.
- **Secure management plane** — administer devices over SSH or HTTPS from a dedicated management network, never over Telnet or HTTP.
- **DNS/DHCP hygiene** — use trusted resolvers, watch for DNS tunneling, and enable DHCP snooping plus dynamic ARP inspection to blunt spoofing.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
1. On a lab Linux VM, set the firewall to default-deny inbound and allow only SSH from your workstation's IP.
2. Add a rule permitting HTTP/HTTPS to a lab web server, then attempt a connection to a blocked port and confirm it is dropped in the firewall log.
3. Sketch a three-zone topology — internet, DMZ, internal — assign subnets, and write the inter-zone rules in plain language.
4. Capture traffic with Wireshark while scanning your own lab host with Nmap; identify the SYN packets and the RST replies on closed ports.
5. Write an IDS-vs-IPS placement note for your sketch: where would each sit, and why? Record everything in your lab notebook.

notes.title: Common mistakes: Secure Network Administration
notes.body:
**Where cybersecurity learners go wrong — and the professional corrections.**

- **Tool-first thinking.** Knowing a scanner's buttons without understanding what the finding *means* produces noise, not security. Learn the underlying concept (e.g., what a vulnerability actually is) before the tool.
- **Checklist compliance mindset.** Controls exist to reduce risk, not to fill spreadsheets. Always ask: what threat does this control actually mitigate?

5. Enable the account's audit trail and locate your own actions in the log. Document each step with its evidence.

modules.summary: Run the first half of a penetration test the professional way. You will follow the standard phases — reconnaissance, scanning, enumeration — against your own lab targets, and learn what a real findings report looks like.
objectives: List the penetration-testing phases in order: reconnaissance, scanning, exploitation, post-exploitation, reporting.

Run vulnerability scans and manually validate findings before reporting them.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Pentest phases in order** — reconnaissance, scanning, exploitation, post-exploitation, reporting. Skipping ahead misses findings.
- **Recon recap** — passive collection first; active probing only inside authorized scope and window.
- **Scanning** — host discovery, port scanning, service/version detection (Nmap is the standard lab tool) to map the attack surface.
- **Vulnerability scanning** — automated scanners (such as Nessus) flag known weaknesses fast, but every finding needs manual validation — scanners produce false positives.
- **Enumeration** — pulling detail from open services (shares, users, banners) to plan precise, authorized tests.
- **Post-exploitation concepts** — document what achieved access would allow (data reach, persistence, lateral movement) to show business impact; in labs, demonstrate without damage.
- **Reporting** — each finding gets a description, evidence, risk rating, and remediation guidance; the report, not the exploit, is the deliverable.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
1. Against your isolated lab target only, run Nmap host discovery and a port scan; record open ports and service versions.
2. Run a vulnerability scan (e.g., Nessus Essentials) against the same target and export the results.
3. Pick one high-severity finding and validate it manually — check the banner or configuration the scanner flagged.
4. Mark any false positives and note why the scanner was wrong.
5. Draft one finding in report format: description, evidence, risk rating, remediation. Save your scans and notes.

notes.body: Write a mini penetration-test report for your lab target: an executive summary (non-technical, one page), a methodology section naming the phases followed, and a findings section with at least three validated findings — each with description, evidence, risk rating, and remediation steps. Close with a remediation priority table. Lab targets only; never real-world systems.

modules.title: Penetration Testing, Part 2
modules.summary: Post-exploitation is where access turns into answers: escalation, movement, and evidence — all inside a written scope. You will practice the second half of a professional pentest: pivoting, lateral movement, persistence with full teardown, and a client-grade report. Everything here assumes authorized testing only.
objectives: Escalate privileges in a lab environment using common misconfigurations and document each step
Pivot through a compromised host to enumerate an otherwise unreachable internal subnet
Demonstrate lateral movement and persistence, then fully tear down all artifacts with peer verification
Write a concise penetration test report with severity-rated findings and remediation guidance

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Post-exploitation** — the phase after initial access is confirmed: enumerating users, shares, and services to determine blast radius, strictly within the written scope.
- **Privilege escalation** — moving from a low-privilege account to administrator or root via misconfigurations or weak service permissions.
- **Pivoting** — routing the tester's traffic through a compromised host to reach internal networks that are not directly reachable.
- **Lateral movement** — advancing host to host using harvested credentials and trusted protocols (SMB, RDP, WinRM); this is why credential hygiene matters.
- **Persistence** — maintaining re-entry through legitimate mechanisms like scheduled tasks; every mechanism must be documented and removed at teardown.
- **Teardown and reporting** — the non-negotiable closeout: all artifacts removed with client confirmation, then severity-ranked findings with evidence, impact, and remediation; the report is the deliverable.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Using a lab network of virtual machines you own (Kali Linux attacker, intentionally vulnerable target):
1. Obtain a low-privilege shell on the target through a known-vulnerable service in the lab.
2. Enumerate: users, groups, shares, running services, scheduled tasks, and local security policy.
3. Identify one misconfiguration that permits privilege escalation and escalate to SYSTEM or root.
4. From the foothold, scan the second subnet reachable only through the compromised host and pivot to it.
5. Document every command with timestamps in a journal as you go.
6. Tear down: remove all created accounts and artifacts, reset the target, and have a peer verify the restore.
Rule: if a step would touch a system outside your lab, it is out of scope — stop and document the boundary.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Produce a penetration test report for the lab engagement: executive summary in business language, methodology, findings table with severity ratings and affected hosts, timestamped evidence, remediation guidance per finding, and a retest section confirming each issue is resolved after fixes. Cap the report at 8 pages — clients pay for clarity, not volume. Attach your teardown checklist, signed off by your peer reviewer.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Phishing** — fraudulent messages impersonating trusted senders to steal credentials or deliver malware; the most common initial-access vector.
- **Spear phishing** — phishing tailored to a specific person or role using researched details; far harder to spot.
- **Pretexting** — inventing a scenario (auditor, vendor, IT support) to make a target volunteer information or access.
- **Vishing / smishing** — voice and SMS phishing; caller ID and sender names are trivially spoofed.
- **OSINT** — public posts, bios, and breach data harvested to personalize lures; shrink your footprint.
- **Indicators** — manufactured urgency, lookalike domains, mismatched display names, unexpected attachments, requests bypassing normal process.
- **Defenses** — phishing-resistant MFA, out-of-band verification, one-click report button, blameless reporting culture.
- **Simulation ethics** — written permission, defined targets, strict data limits, immediate support for anyone who clicks.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure

notes.title: Common mistakes: Social Engineering
notes.body:
**Where cybersecurity learners go wrong — and the professional corrections.**

- **Tool-first thinking.** Knowing a scanner's buttons without understanding what the finding *means* produces noise, not security. Learn the underlying concept (e.g., what a vulnerability actually is) before the tool.

- **No documentation habit.** Undocumented findings and actions are un-auditable. Write as if someone else must act on your notes at 3 AM.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Anomaly detection** — unsupervised models flag behavior deviating from baseline; high signal, high noise, needs tuning.
- **Classification** — supervised models label files, emails, and URLs as malicious or benign from labeled examples.
- **SIEM triage** — machine learning ranks and clusters alerts so analysts work the highest-risk items first.
- **Evasion** — adversarial inputs crafted to slip past a model; countered with adversarial training.
- **Data poisoning** — corrupting training data so the model learns wrong; defend with provenance checks.
- **Prompt injection** — malicious instructions hidden in content an AI assistant processes.
- **AI-enabled attacks** — generated phishing, cloned voices, deepfake video; verify via trusted channels.
- **Data leakage** — secrets pasted into public AI tools can leak; use approved private deployments.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
With Python and a small sample dataset in a local sandbox:
1. Compute a baseline of login times and flag outliers with a simple z-score — your hand-rolled anomaly detector.
2. Train a tiny classifier on labeled sample emails and test it on held-out samples; record the false positives.
3. Attempt a prompt-injection test against a local chatbot: hide an instruction inside pasted 'data' and observe whether the model follows it.
4. Study a disclosed synthetic-voice sample and list the verification steps you would require before trusting a voice instruction.
5. Write the tuning note: which alerts you would suppress, which you would escalate, and why.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **GDPR** — EU data-protection regulation: lawful basis for processing, rights of access, erasure, portability; breach notification to authorities within 72 hours.
- **CCPA** — California privacy law: rights to know, delete, and opt out of the sale or sharing of personal information.
- **NIST Privacy Framework** — five functions: Identify, Govern, Control, Communicate, Protect; a voluntary framework.
- **Data classification** — labeling data Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted so handling rules follow the label.
- **Data minimization** — collecting only the personal data a purpose requires; the cheapest breach is data never held.
- **Retention and disposal** — keeping data only as long as needed, then deleting it securely; stale data is liability.
- **Privacy by design** — building protections into systems from the start, not bolting them on later.
- **Third-party risk** — vendors holding your data inherit your obligations; assess via questionnaires, contracts, and reviews.

5. Write five vendor-assessment questions covering encryption, subprocessors, breach notice, data return, and audit rights.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **OT vs IT** — IT manages data; OT manages physical processes. OT prioritizes safety and availability; outages can have physical consequences.
- **Purdue model** — Level 0 physical process; Level 1 devices (sensors, actuators, PLCs); Level 2 control (SCADA, HMIs); Level 3 operations (historians); Level 3.5 DMZ; Level 4 logistics; Level 5 enterprise.
- **PLC** — programmable logic controller: rugged Level 1 computer executing control logic.
- **SCADA / HMI** — Level 2 systems that monitor and direct the industrial process.
- **IT/OT convergence** — connecting control networks to business IT imports IT threats into OT.
- **IoT attack surface** — default credentials, unpatched firmware, insecure protocols like Telnet, often no update path.
- **Segmentation** — isolating OT and IoT networks with firewalls so a compromised laptop cannot reach a controller.
- **Passive monitoring** — observing OT traffic via span ports and taps; active scanning can crash fragile controllers.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
In your home or lab:
1. Inventory every IoT device: list it, confirm the admin password is changed from the default, and note the firmware version.
2. Check for exposed management services (Telnet, HTTP admin) from your own network and close or restrict what you find.
3. Move IoT devices to a separate guest network or VLAN, isolated from your main devices.
4. On paper, map a fictional bottling plant to Purdue levels 0–5, placing each device and system.
5. Write a monitoring plan: capture points, what 'normal' traffic looks like, and the rule — no active scans against control devices.

notes.title: Common mistakes: OT and IoT Risk
notes.body:
**Where cybersecurity learners go wrong — and the professional corrections.**

- **Tool-first thinking.** Knowing a scanner's buttons without understanding what the finding *means* produces noise, not security. Learn the underlying concept (e.g., what a vulnerability actually is) before the tool.
- **Checklist compliance mindset.** Controls exist to reduce risk, not to fill spreadsheets. Always ask: what threat does this control actually mitigate?
- **Ignoring the human layer.** Most breaches involve human factors; a purely technical view misses phishing, misconfiguration, and process failures.
- **Absolute language.** 'Unhackable', '100% secure', 'zero risk' — none of these exist. Security is risk management under uncertainty; speak in likelihoods and trade-offs.
- **No documentation habit.** Undocumented findings and actions are un-auditable. Write as if someone else must act on your notes at 3 AM.

notes.title: Why this math matters for Cybersecurity Professional
notes.body:
**Relevance.** Cryptography is number theory: RSA, Diffie-Hellman, and hashing all rest on primes and modular arithmetic. This module builds that foundation.

Work this module before the technical modules it supports: the worked examples below are fully computed (verify each with the Python lab), and the drills test the exact calculations you will reuse. Math done by hand once beats math skimmed ten times.

notes.title: Divisibility, primes, and factorization
notes.body: a divides b (a|b) if b = ak for some integer k. A prime has exactly two divisors (1 and itself); 1 is neither prime nor composite. The Fundamental Theorem: every integer > 1 factors uniquely into primes. Worked example (verified): factor 360. 360 = 36×10 = (2²×3²)×(2×5) = 2³·3²×5. Check: 8×9×5 = 360 ✓. Divisibility tests: by 3 iff digit sum divisible by 3 (360: 3+6+0=9 ✓); by 11 via alternating sum. Trial division up to √n decides primality for small n: to test 97, trial primes ≤ √97 ≈ 9.8, i.e., 2,3,5,7 — none divide, so 97 is prime. Cryptography’s asymmetry lives here: multiplying primes is trivial, factoring the product is (classically) hard.

notes.title: The gcd and Euclid’s algorithm
notes.body: gcd(a,b) is the largest d dividing both. Euclid: gcd(a,b) = gcd(b, a mod b), recurse until remainder 0. Worked example (verified): gcd(48,18). 48 = 2×18+12; 18 = 1×12+6; 12 = 2×6+0 ⇒ gcd = 6. Check: divisors of 48 include 6, of 18 include 6; nothing larger divides both ✓. The algorithm runs in O(log min(a,b)) steps — ancient (c. 300 BCE) and still optimal in practice. Extended Euclid also finds x,y with ax+by = gcd(a,b) (Bézout’s identity), which is how RSA computes modular inverses: d with ed ≡ 1 (mod φ(n)). Whenever you need "the largest shared structure" — key sizes, cycle alignment, fraction reduction — Euclid is the tool.

notes.title: Modular arithmetic
notes.body: a ≡ b (mod m) means m divides a−b; work with remainders 0..m−1. Addition/multiplication carry over: (a+b) mod m, (a·b) mod m. Powers reduce via repeated squaring. Worked examples (verified): 17+25 mod 12: 42 mod 12 = 6 (42 = 3×12+6) ✓. 3^4 mod 7: 81 mod 7 = 4 (81 = 11×7+4) ✓. 2^10 mod 11: 1024 mod 11 = 1 (11×93=1023) ✓ — a preview of Fermat. Hash tables, checksums, and cyclic schedules are modular arithmetic in production: "slot = hash(key) mod table_size" is a congruence, and off-by-one errors there are congruence errors. Warning: division mod m needs a modular inverse, which exists only when gcd(a,m)=1.

notes.title: Fermat’s little theorem and Euler’s theorem
notes.body: Fermat: for prime p and a not divisible by p, a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p). Euler generalizes: a^φ(m) ≡ 1 (mod m) when gcd(a,m)=1, where φ(m) counts 1≤k≤m coprime to m. Worked examples (verified): 5^6 mod 7: p=7 prime, 6 = p−1, so ≡ 1 ✓ (direct: 15625 = 2232×7+1 ✓). φ(12): numbers ≤12 coprime to 12 are 1,5,7,11 ⇒ φ(12) = 4; also 12×(1−1/2)×(1−1/3) = 12×1/2×2/3 = 4 ✓. Then 5^4 mod 12 ≡ 1: 625 = 52×12+1 ✓. These theorems shrink huge exponents: to compute a^1000 mod 7, reduce 1000 mod 6 first. This exponent-shrinking is what makes RSA decryption feasible at all.

notes.title: RSA, sketched honestly
notes.body: Key generation: pick primes p,q; n = pq; φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1); choose e coprime to φ(n); d = e^−1 mod φ(n) (via extended Euclid). Encrypt c = m^e mod n; decrypt m = c^d mod n. Correctness: ed ≡ 1 mod φ(n) so c^d = m^(ed) = m^(1+kφ(n)) ≡ m (mod n) by Euler. Worked toy example (verified): p=5, q=11 ⇒ n=55, φ=40. e=3 (gcd(3,40)=1); d=27 since 3×27=81=2×40+1 ✓. Encrypt m=7: c = 7³ mod 55 = 343 mod 55 = 13 (55×6=330) ✓. Decrypt: 13^27 mod 55 = 7 ✓ (Euler guarantees it; Python confirms). Real RSA uses 2048-bit primes — the toy shows the mechanism, not the security. The hardness assumption: factoring n is infeasible; everything else is arithmetic.

notes.title: Hashing, randomness, and where number theory bites
notes.body: Non-cryptographic hashing leans on modular arithmetic: Python’s tuple hash, Java’s 31×h+c string hash, and FNV all mix via multiply-and-mod. Worked example (verified): FNV-1a-ish toy on "ab" with mod 2^8: h=0; h = (h⊕2)×33+97 mod 256: start 0⊕2=2? (use offset basis 0 for the toy) — concretely: h=((0×33)+97) mod 256 = 97; h=((97×33)+98) mod 256 = (3201+98) mod 256 = 3299 mod 256 = 227 (256×12=3072; 3299−3072=227) ✓. Different strings can collide (pigeonhole); good hashes spread uniformly. Diffie-Hellman key exchange is Fermat/Euler in action: both sides compute g^(ab) mod p from exchanged g^a, g^b — eavesdroppers face the discrete-log problem. Takeaway: whenever data meets "mod", number theory governs correctness and security margins.

cards.back: p prime, p∖|a ⇒ a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p).

cards.front: When does a modular inverse exist?
cards.back: a^−1 mod m exists iff gcd(a,m)=1.

cards.front: Why is factoring relevant to crypto?
cards.back: Multiplying primes is easy; factoring the product is classically hard — RSA’s asymmetry.
gcd(a,m)=1 ⇒ a^φ(m) ≡ 1 (mod m).

quiz.q: Prime factorization of 360?
By Fermat, 5^6 mod 7 = ?
quiz.explain: 5^6 ≡ 1 mod 7 for prime 7.
Coprime residues: 1,5,7,11.

quiz.q: RSA toy: n=55, e=3, d=27. Encrypt m=7:
Which has a modular inverse mod 12?
quiz.explain: gcd(5,12)=1; the others share factors with 12.
1024 = 93×11+1; also Fermat with p=11.

modules.title: Prereq Math: Statistics & Probability for Cybersecurity Professional
modules.summary: Descriptive statistics, probability rules, Bayes’ theorem, expectation and variance, the binomial and normal distributions, and hypothesis testing — the math behind evaluation metrics, alert triage, and A/B decisions. Prerequisite spine for Cybersecurity Professional.
objectives: Compute mean, median, variance, and standard deviation of a dataset.
Apply the addition and multiplication rules of probability.
Use Bayes’ theorem to update beliefs with evidence.
Compute expectation and variance of discrete random variables.

notes.title: Why this math matters for Cybersecurity Professional
notes.body:
**Relevance.** Risk quantification, detection metrics, and security measurement are statistics. This module teaches honest security numbers.

Work this module before the technical modules it supports: the worked examples below are fully computed (verify each with the Python lab), and the drills test the exact calculations you will reuse. Math done by hand once beats math skimmed ten times.

notes.title: Describing data: center and spread
notes.body: For data x₁..xₙ: the mean x̄ = (Σxᵢ)/n; the median is the middle value when sorted; the variance s² = Σ(xᵢ−x̄)²/(n−1) (sample) and standard deviation s = √s². Worked example (verified): response times [12, 15, 13, 90, 14] ms. Mean = (12+15+13+90+14)/5 = 144/5 = 28.8. Median: sorted [12,13,14,15,90] → 14. The single outlier (90) drags the mean to 28.8 while the median stays 14 — this is why latency is reported with medians/percentiles, not means. Deviations from mean: [−16.8, −13.8, −15.8, 61.2, −14.8]; squared sum = 282.24+190.44+249.64+3745.44+219.04 = 4686.8; sample variance = 4686.8/4 = 1171.7; s ≈ 34.2 ms. Report center AND spread together — a mean without spread is a half-truth.

notes.title: Probability rules that never change
notes.body: Sample space S, event A: 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1, P(S) = 1. Addition rule: P(A∪b) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B) (subtract the double-counted overlap); for mutually exclusive events the last term is 0. Complement: P(not A) = 1−P(A). Multiplication: P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B|A); for independent events, P(B|A)=P(B). Worked example (verified): a queue has 30% high-priority tickets (H) and 20% are escalations (E); 12% are both. P(H∪E) = 0.30+0.20−0.12 = 0.38. If instead H and E were independent, P(both) would be 0.30×0.20 = 0.06 ≠ 0.12 — so they are NOT independent (escalations skew high-priority). Two independent deploys each fail with p=0.05: P(both fail) = 0.05² = 0.0025; P(at least one fails) = 1−(0.95)² = 1−0.9025 = 0.0975.

notes.title: Conditional probability and Bayes’ theorem
notes.body: P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B): probability of A given B occurred. Bayes inverts the conditioning: P(D|+) = P(+|D)P(D)/P(+). Worked example — alert triage (verified): 1% of hosts are compromised (P(D)=0.01). The detector catches 99% of compromised hosts (sensitivity P(+|D)=0.99) and false-alarms on 5% of clean hosts (P(+|¬D)=0.05). P(+) = 0.99×0.01 + 0.05×0.99 = 0.0099+0.0495 = 0.0594. P(D|+) = 0.0099/0.0594 ≈ 0.1667 — only ~16.7%! Most alerts are false positives despite a "99% accurate" detector, because the base rate is tiny. This base-rate effect is the single most important probability lesson for SOC triage, medical screening, and fraud detection: accuracy without the base rate is meaningless. Always expand P(+) via total probability before trusting a positive.

notes.title: Expectation and variance of random variables
notes.body: For discrete X with values xᵢ and probabilities pᵢ: E[X] = Σxᵢpᵢ (long-run average); Var(X) = E[X²]−(E[X])²; SD = √Var. Linearity: E[aX+b] = aE[X]+b, and E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y] even when dependent. Worked example — fair die (verified): E[X] = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 21/6 = 3.5. E[X²] = (1+4+9+16+25+36)/6 = 91/6 ≈ 15.1667. Var = 91/6 − 3.5² = 15.1667−12.25 = 2.9167 = 35/12. SD ≈ 1.708. Worked example 2: a Bernoulli trial with success p has E[X]=p and Var=p(1−p) — variance peaks at p=0.5 (maximum uncertainty). In ML, cross-entropy loss is minimized exactly when predicted probabilities match these expectations; in capacity planning, E[load] sizes the average but Var(load) sizes the headroom.

notes.title: The binomial and normal distributions
notes.body: Binomial(n,p): number of successes in n independent trials; P(X=k) = C(n,k)p^k(1−p)^(n−k), E[X]=np, Var=np(1−p). Normal(μ,σ²): the bell curve; the 68-95-99.7 rule says P(|X−μ|<σ)≈0.68, <2σ ≈0.95, <3σ ≈0.997. Worked example — binomial (verified): 5 independent alert rules, each fires spuriously with p=0.3. P(exactly 2 fire) = C(5,2)·0.3²·0.7³ = 10×0.09×0.343 = 0.3087 ≈ 30.9%. Worked example — normal: API latency ~ Normal(μ=120ms, σ=15ms). P(latency > 150) = P(Z > 2) ≈ 0.0228 — about 2.3% of requests. The Central Limit Theorem is why the normal appears everywhere: averages of many small independent effects are approximately normal, which justifies z-intervals for A/B test readouts and poll margins.

notes.title: Hypothesis testing and confidence, honestly
notes.body: A hypothesis test asks: "is this data surprising under the null hypothesis H₀?" The p-value is P(data this extreme | H₀) — NOT P(H₀ is true). Reject H₀ when p < α (often 0.05). A 95% confidence interval is a procedure that covers the true parameter in 95% of repetitions — not "95% chance the truth is inside this interval". Worked example (verified): conversion rate baseline 10% (H₀: p=0.10). In n=400 trials we observe 52 conversions (ς=0.13). SE = √(0.1×0.9/400) = √(0.000225) = 0.015. z = (0.13−0.10)/0.015 = 2.0. Two-sided p ≈ 0.0455 < 0.05 — reject H₀; the lift is statistically significant. But "significant" ≠ important: a 3-point lift may not cover the feature’s cost. Report effect size and confidence interval alongside every p-value, pre-register the hypothesis (no p-hacking), and remember that with 20 metrics tested, one will be "significant" by chance alone.

cards.back: Mean = Σx/n (pulled by outliers: [12,15,13,90,14] → 28.8); median = middle value (14) — robust.
s² = Σ(xᵢ−x̄)²/(n−1); standard deviation s = √s².
P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). Subtract the overlap; mutually exclusive ⇒ last term 0.
P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B), equivalently P(B|A) = P(B).
P(D|+) = P(+|D)P(D)/P(+), with P(+) expanded by total probability.
With 1% prevalence and 5% false-alarm rate, P(compromised|alert) ≈ 16.7% — most alerts are false.

cards.front: E[X] and Var(X) for a fair die?

cards.back: C(n,k)p^k(1−p)^(n−k); E[X]=np, Var=np(1−p).
For Normal(μ,σ): ≈68% within 1σ, 95% within 2σ, 99.7% within 3σ of μ.
P(data this extreme | H₀) — not P(H₀ true). Reject H₀ when p < α.

cards.front: z for ς=0.13 vs H₀ p=0.10, n=400?
cards.back: SE=0.015, z=2.0, two-sided p≈0.0455 — significant at α=0.05.

cards.front: Why report effect size with p-values?
cards.back: "Significant" ≠ important; with 20 metrics tested, one hits p<0.05 by chance.

choices: Median — the outlier 90 distorts the mean
quiz.explain: The single 90 nearly doubles the mean; the median (14) resists it. Latency is reported with medians/percentiles for this reason.
0.30+0.20−0.12 = 0.38. (0.06 would assume independence — but 0.12 ≠ 0.06, so they are dependent.)

Fair die: E[X²]?
5 alert rules, each spurious-fires w.p. 0.3 independently. P(exactly 2 fire)?
Latency ~ N(120, 15²) ms. P(latency > 150)?
H₀: p=0.10, n=400, observed ς=0.13. z and conclusion at α=0.05?
A 95% confidence interval means:
choices: 95% chance the true value is inside this interval
The procedure covers the truth in 95% of repetitions
quiz.explain: Frequentist coverage is about the procedure’s long-run behavior, not a probability on this specific interval.

handsOnLab.brief: You will verify the Bayes triage calculation, the binomial probability, and the die variance three ways: by hand formula, by exact computation, and by Monte Carlo simulation. All three must agree.
steps: Open python3. Simulate the Bayes scenario: 1M hosts, 1% compromised; detector: 99% sensitivity, 5% false-alarm. Count positives and the fraction compromised among them; confirm ≈0.167.

modules.title: Prereq Math: Logic & Proof for Cybersecurity Professional
modules.summary: Propositional logic, truth tables, quantifiers, and the four proof methods (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, induction) — the reasoning substrate for policies, algorithms, and security arguments. Prerequisite spine for Cybersecurity Professional.
objectives: Evaluate compound propositions with truth tables and identify tautologies.
Apply De Morgan’s laws and logical equivalences to simplify statements.
Negate quantified statements correctly (∀/∃ duality).
Write direct, contrapositive, contradiction, and induction proofs.

notes.title: Why this math matters for Cybersecurity Professional
notes.body:
**Relevance.** Access control, policy analysis, and security proofs are logic. This module gives you the formal methods.

Work this module before the technical modules it supports: the worked examples below are fully computed (verify each with the Python lab), and the drills test the exact calculations you will reuse. Math done by hand once beats math skimmed ten times.

notes.title: Propositions, connectives, and truth tables
notes.body: A proposition is a statement that is either true (T) or false (F) — never both. The connectives build compounds: negation ¬p, conjunction p∧q (and), disjunction p∨q (or, inclusive), implication p→q (if p then q), biconditional p↔q (p iff q). A truth table enumerates every input combination: n variables need 2^n rows. Worked example: build the table for p→q. Recall p→q is F only when p=T and q=F. Rows: (T,T)→T; (T,F)→F; (F,T)→T; (F,F)→T. So "if 2+2=5 then the moon is cheese" is TRUE as a material implication — the antecedent is false. This surprises beginners, but implication promises only that a true antecedent never yields a false consequent. In policy engines and code (if-statements), this is exactly the semantics: the rule fires only when the condition holds; a false condition makes the implication vacuously true.

notes.title: Tautologies, contradictions, and De Morgan’s laws
notes.body: A tautology is true in every row (e.g., p∨¬p); a contradiction is false in every row (p∧¬p). Two formulas are logically equivalent if their tables match column-for-column. Worked example (verified): prove De Morgan’s law ¬(p∧q) ≡ ¬p∨¬q by table. Row (T,T): LHS ¬T=F; RHS F∨F=F. Row (T,F): LHS ¬F=T; RHS F∨T=T. Row (F,T): LHS T; RHS T∨F=T. Row (F,F): LHS T; RHS T∨T=T. All four rows agree — equivalence verified. The dual law ¬(p∨q) ≡ ¬p∧¬q holds by the same check. These laws are the workhorses of simplifying firewall rules, IAM policies, and boolean search: "not (A and B)" becomes "not-A or not-B". Other key equivalences: contrapositive (p→q ≡ ¬q→¬p), and implication-as-disjunction (p→q ≡ ¬p∨q).

notes.title: Predicates and quantifiers
notes.body: A predicate P(x) becomes a proposition when x is fixed. Quantifiers bind x: ∀x P(x) ("for all x") and ∃x P(x) ("there exists x"). Worked example: let domain be integers, P(x) = "x² ≥ 0". Then ∀x P(x) is TRUE (squares are never negative). Now negate ∀x∃y (y > x) — "for every integer there is a larger one". Negation flips each quantifier and the inner predicate: ∃x∀y (y ≤ x) — "some integer is ≥ every integer", which is FALSE over integers (no maximum). The duality rules: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x), and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). Common error: negating "all users are admins" as "no users are admins" — the correct negation is "some user is not an admin". In access-control requirements, this distinction is the difference between a correct policy and a breach.

notes.title: Direct proof and proof by contrapositive
notes.body: A direct proof assumes the hypothesis and derives the conclusion through valid steps. Proof by contrapositive proves ¬q→¬p instead of p→q (equivalent by the table). Worked example: prove "if n² is even, then n is even" for integers. Direct attack stalls (square roots of parity are awkward), so use contrapositive: "if n is odd, then n² is odd". Let n = 2k+1. Then n² = 4k²+4k+1 = 2(2k²+2k)+1, which is odd. Contrapositive proved, so the original holds. Numeric check: n=7 (odd) → 49 (odd) ✓; n=6 (even) → 36 (even) ✓. Choose the method by shape: when the conclusion is a negative or "not" statement, contrapositive usually simplifies; when hypothesis and conclusion are both positive constructions, go direct.

notes.title: Proof by contradiction
notes.body: Assume the negation of what you want, derive an impossibility, and conclude the original. Worked example (classic, verified): prove √2 is irrational. Assume √2 = a/b in lowest terms (gcd(a,b)=1). Then 2 = a²/b², so a² = 2b² — a² is even, hence a is even (by the previous note’s result), a = 2k. Then 4k² = 2b², so b² = 2k² — b² is even, hence b is even. But a and b both even contradicts lowest terms. The assumption is impossible; √2 is irrational. The pattern: contradiction proofs shine when the claim says something does NOT exist (no rational square root, no largest prime). Euclid’s proof of infinitely many primes uses the same skeleton: assume finitely many, multiply them and add 1, find a new prime factor — contradiction.

notes.title: Mathematical induction
notes.body: To prove P(n) for all n ≥ n₀: (1) base case P(n₀); (2) inductive step: assume P(k) (induction hypothesis), prove P(k+1). Worked example (verified): prove 1+2+⋯+n = n(n+1)/2. Base n=1: LHS 1, RHS 1·2/2 = 1 ✓. Assume true for k. For k+1: LHS = k(k+1)/2 + (k+1) = (k+1)(k/2+1) = (k+1)(k+2)/2 ✓ — exactly the formula at n=k+1. Numeric spot-check: n=5 gives 1+2+3+4+5=15 and 5·6/2=15 ✓; n=100 gives 5050 = 100×101/2 ✓. Induction is the proof method behind every loop-correctness argument and every recursive algorithm analysis: the base case is the loop’s first iteration, the step is "if the invariant holds entering iteration k, it holds leaving it".

cards.back: A statement that is unambiguously true or false — never both, never neither.
Only when p is true and q is false. All other rows are true (vacuous truth).
¬(p∧q) ≡ ¬p∨¬q and ¬(p∨q) ≡ ¬p∧¬q — verified by truth table.
∃x ¬P(x). Quantifier flips; inner predicate negates.

cards.front: What is the contrapositive of p→q?
cards.back: ¬q→¬p — logically equivalent to the original.

cards.front: p→q is equivalent to which disjunction?
cards.back: ¬p∨q.

cards.front: What is a tautology? A contradiction?
cards.back: Tautology: true in every truth-table row (p∨¬p). Contradiction: false in every row (p∧¬p).
Assume the negation of the claim; derive an impossibility; conclude the claim holds.

cards.front: The two steps of mathematical induction?
cards.back: Base case P(n₀); inductive step: P(k) ⇒ P(k+1).

cards.front: Prove: if n² is even then n is even. Method?
cards.back: Contrapositive: n odd ⇒ n=2k+1 ⇒ n²=2(2k²+2k)+1, odd.

quiz.q: p=F, q=T. What is p→q?
quiz.explain: Implication is false only for (T,F). With a false antecedent it is vacuously true.

quiz.q: ¬(p∨q) is equivalent to:
quiz.explain: De Morgan’s second law — verified row-by-row in the notes.

quiz.q: The contrapositive of "If the alert fires, the SOC investigates" is:
choices: If the alert does not fire, the SOC does not investigate
If the SOC does not investigate, the alert did not fire
If the SOC investigates, the alert fired
The alert fires iff the SOC investigates
quiz.explain: Contrapositive flips and negates: ¬q→¬p. (The first choice is the inverse — a different, non-equivalent statement.)

quiz.q: Negation of "Every admin has MFA enabled":
choices: Some admin does not have MFA enabled
quiz.explain: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x). "None do" is stronger than the negation and usually false.

quiz.q: Which is a tautology?
quiz.explain: For any p,q, at least one direction of implication holds — check all four rows. The others fail on some row.

quiz.q: To prove "there is no largest prime" you would use:
quiz.explain: Non-existence claims suit contradiction: assume finitely many primes, construct a number with a new prime factor.

quiz.q: In an induction proof of 1+⋯+n=n(n+1)/2, the inductive step shows:
quiz.explain: Assume the hypothesis at k, derive k+1: k(k+1)/2+(k+1) = (k+1)(k+2)/2.

quiz.q: p=T, q=F. Evaluate (p→q)∨(q→p).
quiz.explain: p→q is F, but q→p is T (false antecedent), and F∨T = T.

quiz.q: "If n is divisible by 4 then n is even." The converse is:
choices: If n is even then n is divisible by 4
If n is not divisible by 4 then n is odd
If n is odd then n is not divisible by 4
n is divisible by 4 iff n is even
quiz.explain: Converse swaps p and q (q→p). It is FALSE (6 is even, not divisible by 4) — converse is not equivalent to the original.

items.answer: Yes — q∧¬q is a contradiction (always F), and p∨F ≡ p.
items.explain: Absorption-style simplification via truth table.

items.prompt: Name the method: assume √3 rational, derive a contradiction.
items.answer: Proof by contradiction.
items.explain: Non-existence/irrationality claims use this skeleton.

items.prompt: Prove "if n is odd then n² is odd" directly (one line).

items.prompt: Induction: state P(k+1) for P(n)="Σi³ = [n(n+1)/2]²".

items.answer: Direct proof: a/b + c/d = (ad+bc)/bd.

items.answer: If x≠2 and x≠−2 then x²≠4.

items.prompt: Base case check: is 2^n > n² true at n=5?
items.explain: Always verify the base numerically before the inductive step.

handsOnLab.title: Verify logic by brute force with Python
handsOnLab.brief: You will verify De Morgan’s laws and the contrapositive equivalence by exhaustive truth-table enumeration in Python, then prove a small parity claim both by hand and by exhaustive check. The machine settles every row; your hand proof must agree.
steps: Open python3. Define implies = lambda p,q: (not p) or q.
Enumerate all four (p,q) pairs. For each, compute not (p and q) and (not p) or (not q); assert they are equal on every row — De Morgan verified by brute force.
Repeat for the dual law: not (p or q) vs (not p) and (not q). Assert equality on all rows.
Verify contrapositive: for all rows, implies(p,q) == implies(not q, not p). Print any counterexample (there will be none).
Show the converse is NOT equivalent: find the row where implies(p,q) != implies(q,p). Record it.
Prove by hand on paper: "if n² is odd then n is odd" via contrapositive. Then brute-force check n in range(0,50): assert (n*n % 2 == 1) implies (n % 2 == 1).
Write up: which equivalences held on all rows, the converse counterexample row, and your parity proof.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A short write-up with the brute-force verification output, the converse counterexample, and the hand parity proof.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: All assertions pass; the converse counterexample row is identified; the hand proof matches the brute-force check.

mockTask.q: A policy states: "If the device is unmanaged, then access is denied." Which restatement is logically equivalent?
choices: If access is granted, then the device is managed
If the device is managed, then access is granted
If access is denied, then the device is unmanaged
Devices are either managed or denied
mockTask.explain: Contrapositive (¬q→¬p) is equivalent. The second is the converse, the third the inverse — neither is equivalent.
