scriptLabs.title: iptables Firewall Rule Lab
scriptLabs.brief: Build a default-deny host firewall: allow loopback and established traffic, expose SSH only to the admin subnet.
scriptLabs.starter:
#!/bin/bash
# Host firewall: default DENY on INPUT, SSH (22) only from 10.0.0.0/8, HTTPS (443) public.
# YOUR CODE HERE: flush rules, set default policies, then add rules in the right order.
# 1. Flush existing rules
# 2. Set INPUT and FORWARD default policy to DROP
# 3. Allow loopback traffic
# 4. Allow ESTABLISHED,RELATED return traffic
# 5. Allow SSH from 10.0.0.0/8 only
# 6. Allow HTTPS from anywhere
# 7. List the final ruleset with counters
scriptLabs.hint: Order matters: loopback first, then the ESTABLISHED,RELATED rule so return traffic is accepted, then the narrow allow rules. Default policies are set with -P; rules are appended with -A.
scriptLabs.solution:
#!/bin/bash
set -e
# 1. Flush existing rules
iptables -F
iptables -X
# 2. Default-deny on INPUT and FORWARD
iptables -P INPUT DROP
iptables -P FORWARD DROP
iptables -P OUTPUT ACCEPT
# 3. Loopback
iptables -A INPUT -i lo -j ACCEPT
# 4. Established / related return traffic
iptables -A INPUT -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
# 5. SSH only from the admin subnet
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp -s 10.0.0.0/8 --dport 22 -m conntrack --ctstate NEW -j ACCEPT
# 6. Public HTTPS
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -m conntrack --ctstate NEW -j ACCEPT
# 7. Review
iptables -L -n -v --line-numbers

scriptLabs.title: Auth-Log Triage with grep
scriptLabs.brief: Hunt a brute-force attack in /var/log/auth.log: count failures, rank attacking IPs, spot successes.
scriptLabs.starter:
#!/bin/bash
LOG=/var/log/auth.log
# YOUR CODE HERE:
# 1. Count total "Failed password" lines
# 2. Rank the top 10 source IPs by failure count
# 3. List distinct usernames targeted
# 4. Show any successful logins ("Accepted") with user, IP, and time
# 5. Check whether any attacking IP later succeeded
scriptLabs.hint: The source IP is the second-to-last field ($(NF-3)) on 'Failed password' lines. Pipe grep into awk, then sort | uniq -c | sort -nr for a ranked attacker list.
scriptLabs.solution:
#!/bin/bash
LOG=/var/log/auth.log
echo "== total failed passwords =="
grep -c "Failed password" "$LOG"
echo "== top 10 attacking IPs =="
grep "Failed password" "$LOG" | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -10
echo "== targeted usernames =="
grep "Failed password" "$LOG" | awk '{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) if($i=="for") print $(i+1)}' | sort -u
echo "== successful logins =="
grep "Accepted" "$LOG" | awk '{print $1, $2, $3, $9, $11}'
echo "== did any attacker IP later succeed? =="
for ip in $(grep "Failed password" "$LOG" | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort -u); do
  grep "Accepted" "$LOG" | grep -q "$ip" && echo "SUCCESS FROM ATTACKER IP: $ip"
done
echo "triage complete"

scriptLabs.title: Phishing Email Header Analysis
scriptLabs.brief: Read raw mail headers in Python: trace Received hops and evaluate SPF, DKIM, and DMARC results.
scriptLabs.starter:
RAW = """Received: from mail.evil-example.com (unknown [203.0.113.77])\n\tby mx.victim.test with ESMTP\nReceived: from [192.0.2.10] by mail.evil-example.com\nFrom: \"CEO\" <ceo@victim.test>\nAuthentication-Results: mx.victim.test; spf=fail smtp.mailfrom=evil-example.com;\n\tdkim=none; dmarc=fail header.from=victim.test"""

def analyze(raw):
    # YOUR CODE HERE:
    # 1. Collect the Received: hops in order (top = last hop)
    # 2. Pull spf=, dkim=, dmarc= verdicts from Authentication-Results
    # 3. Compare the From: domain to the envelope sender domain
    # 4. Return/print a verdict: LIKELY PHISH or CLEAN, with reasons
    pass

analyze(RAW)
scriptLabs.hint: The topmost Received header is the last hop (your server). A From domain that doesn't match the envelope sender plus spf=fail and dmarc=fail is the classic spoofing pattern.
scriptLabs.solution:
RAW = "\n".join([
"Received: from mail.evil-example.com (unknown [203.0.113.77])",
"\tby mx.victim.test with ESMTP",
"Received: from [192.0.2.10] by mail.evil-example.com",
'From: "CEO" <ceo@victim.test>',
"Authentication-Results: mx.victim.test; spf=fail smtp.mailfrom=evil-example.com;",
"\tdkim=none; dmarc=fail header.from=victim.test",
])

def analyze(raw):
    reasons = []
    unfolded = raw.replace("\n\t", " ").replace("\n ", " ")
    lines = unfolded.split("\n")
    hops = [l[len("Received:"):].strip() for l in lines if l.startswith("Received:")]
    print("Hops (last hop first):")
    for h in hops:
        print("  -", h[:70])
    auth = " ".join(l for l in lines if l.startswith("Authentication-Results:"))
    low = auth.lower()
    def verdict(key):
        i = low.find(key)
        return low[i + len(key):].split(";")[0].split()[0] if i != -1 else "missing"
    spf, dkim, dmarc = verdict("spf="), verdict("dkim="), verdict("dmarc=")
    print("SPF:", spf, "| DKIM:", dkim, "| DMARC:", dmarc)
    if spf == "fail":
        reasons.append("SPF fail: sending IP not authorized for envelope domain")
    if dmarc == "fail":
        reasons.append("DMARC fail: From domain not aligned with authenticated sender")
    if dkim == "none":
        reasons.append("No DKIM signature present")
    from_line = next((l for l in lines if l.startswith("From:")), "")
    env_domain = low.split("smtp.mailfrom=")[-1].split(";")[0].strip()
    from_domain = from_line.split("@")[-1].strip().rstrip(">")
    if from_domain and env_domain and from_domain != env_domain:
        reasons.append("From domain (%s) mismatches envelope sender (%s)" % (from_domain, env_domain))
    print("VERDICT:", "LIKELY PHISH - " + "; ".join(reasons) if reasons else "CLEAN")

analyze(RAW)

drills.title: CIA Triad: Confidentiality
drills.prompt: Encrypting customer data at rest primarily protects which leg of the CIA triad?
drills.explain: Confidentiality means only authorized parties can read data; encryption is its primary technical control. (Module 2)

drills.title: NIST CSF 2.0 Functions
drills.prompt: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 organizes cybersecurity outcomes into how many Functions?
drills.explain: CSF 2.0 has six Functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. (Module 3)

drills.title: Firewall Default Policy
drills.prompt: The recommended default firewall posture is:
choices: Allow all traffic, then block known-bad ports
Deny all traffic, then allow only what is needed
Allow all outbound and all inbound
drills.explain: Default deny (deny all, allow by exception) minimizes the attack surface; allowlists beat blocklists. (Module 7)

drills.title: Password Storage
drills.prompt: Which is an appropriate choice for storing password hashes?
drills.explain: bcrypt is an adaptive, salted password-hashing function; MD5/SHA-1 are fast unsalted digests, and Base64 is not hashing at all. (Module 8)

drills.title: Initial Access Vector
drills.prompt: Which remains one of the most common initial access vectors in real-world breaches?
choices: Guessing the Wi-Fi password from the parking lot
drills.explain: Phishing — especially spearphishing with malicious links or attachments — is a perennial top initial access vector. (Module 4)

drills.title: Least Privilege
drills.prompt: The principle of least privilege states that users and processes should:
choices: Share one admin account for efficiency
Have standing domain-admin rights just in case
Log in as root by default
Receive only the minimum access needed for their tasks
drills.explain: Least privilege limits blast radius: grant the minimum access required, nothing more. (Module 6)

drills.title: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic
choices: The adversary's tactical goal — the 'why' of an action
drills.explain: Tactics are the adversary's objectives (e.g., Initial Access, Exfiltration); techniques are the 'how'. (Module 4)

drills.title: 3-2-1 Backup Rule
choices: 3 copies of data, on 2 different media, with 1 copy offsite
Back up 3 times a day for 2 weeks, keep 1 year
drills.explain: Three copies, two media types, one offsite/offline copy — the offline copy defeats ransomware encryption of backups. (Module 10)

drills.title: DMARC Purpose
choices: A published policy telling receivers how to handle mail that fails SPF/DKIM alignment
A password manager for email accounts
drills.explain: DMARC lets a domain owner publish handling policy (none/quarantine/reject) for unauthenticated mail plus reporting. (Module 7)

drills.title: Risk Definition
choices: A function of threat, vulnerability, and impact
Something eliminated by buying a firewall
drills.explain: Risk = the potential for loss, commonly modeled as threat x vulnerability x impact. (Module 1)

drills.title: Risk scoring
drills.prompt: Threat=4, Vulnerability=5, Impact=2. Risk priority vs T=2,V=2,I=5?
drills.explain: 40 vs 20 on the T×V×I product. High impact alone doesn't outrank likely exploitation of moderate impact — multiply, don't eyeball.

drills.title: CSF function
drills.prompt: Deploying EDR across the fleet maps to which CSF 2.0 function?
drills.explain: EDR hardens endpoints (Protect) and generates detections (Detect). CSF functions overlap by design — map to all that apply.

drills.title: IR order
drills.explain: Preparation first (it's a phase, not a prelude), then the lifecycle, then post-incident learning.

drills.title: Kill chain break
drills.prompt: Email gateway blocks the malicious attachment. Which kill-chain phase broke?
drills.explain: Delivery = getting the weapon to the target. Blocking it there is the cheapest break in the chain.

drills.title: Board communication
drills.prompt: The board asks about a critical CVE. Best framing?
choices: Business terms: exposure ($/downtime/regulatory), remediation time, residual risk after patching
drills.explain: Risk in business language with a remediation plan. Technical detail goes in the appendix.

scenarios.title: Ransomware IR Tabletop
scenarios.context: Friday 6:40 PM: the help desk reports finance file shares renamed with .locked extensions and a ransom note on the file server. EDR shows SMB lateral movement from an accounting workstation. You are the incident commander at a 25-person company with nightly backups that have never had a restore tested.

steps.prompt: First 30 minutes: what is your immediate containment move?

options.text: Isolate the affected hosts from the network (unplug/disable switch ports, EDR network quarantine), but leave them powered on
options.why: Isolation stops lateral spread while preserving volatile memory and logs for forensics.

options.text: Power off the entire data center immediately
options.why: A blind shutdown destroys volatile evidence and causes unnecessary outage for unaffected systems.

options.text: Pay the ransom right away to minimize downtime
options.why: Paying funds criminals, has no guarantee of recovery, and skips containment entirely.

options.text: Wait until Monday so the full team is available
options.why: Ransomware spreads in minutes; delay guarantees wider encryption.

steps.prompt: The ransom note demands 2 BTC within 72 hours. The CFO asks whether to pay. Your recommendation?

options.text: Pay quickly — downtime costs more than the ransom
options.why: Payment does not guarantee working decryptors and marks you as a willing payer for future attacks.

options.text: Refuse to pay; recover from verified clean backups after confirming they are intact and offline
options.why: Restoration from clean, tested backups is the reliable path; law-enforcement guidance also discourages payment.

options.text: Negotiate directly over personal email to buy time
options.why: Engaging the actor risks further extortion and complicates any law-enforcement involvement.

options.text: Delete all encrypted files and start over
options.why: Deletion destroys both data and forensic evidence with no recovery benefit.

steps.prompt: Before rebuilding systems, what must happen to preserve the investigation?

options.text: Reimage everything immediately to get users working
options.why: Reimaging wipes forensic artifacts needed to determine scope and entry point.

options.text: Capture forensic images and export logs (EDR, firewall, auth) before rebuilding, maintaining chain of custody
options.why: Preserved evidence lets you confirm scope, find patient zero, and support legal/insurance needs.

options.text: Wipe the logs to free disk space for the rebuild
options.why: Log destruction eliminates the timeline you need to verify eradication.

options.text: Only back up the ransom note as a souvenir
options.why: The note alone reveals nothing about scope, persistence, or data theft.

steps.prompt: Two weeks later, systems are restored. What closes out the incident properly?

options.text: Declare victory and change nothing
options.why: Without changes, the same attack path remains open.

options.text: Blame the accountant whose workstation was patient zero
options.why: Blame cultures suppress future reporting; the failure was systemic.

options.text: Run a blameless post-incident review, test backup restores, and close the gaps (email filtering, patching, segmentation)
options.why: Lessons-learned with concrete remediation and tested restores is the core of the post-incident phase.

options.text: Buy a new firewall and assume the problem is solved
options.why: A single product purchase is not a remediation plan and ignores the actual root causes.

scenarios.title: Phishing Campaign Defense
scenarios.context: Three employees report an email spoofing the CEO requesting gift-card purchases. Headers show SPF fail and no DKIM signature. Two users clicked the link and entered their corporate credentials before the page was taken down.

steps.prompt: How do you triage the reported message?

options.text: Delete the reports — users overreact
options.why: Dismissing reports kills the human sensor network you depend on.

options.text: Analyze headers and URLs, detonate the link in a sandbox, and extract indicators (sender, URLs, hashes)
options.why: Header analysis plus safe detonation yields IOCs for containment without endangering anyone.

options.text: Forward the phishing email to the whole company as a warning
options.why: Forwarding live phish spreads the malicious link to more inboxes.

options.text: Reply to the sender asking them to stop
options.why: Engaging the attacker confirms active targets and accomplishes nothing.

steps.prompt: Containment for the two compromised accounts — what is the right sequence?

options.text: Force password resets, revoke active sessions/tokens, block the IOCs at the email gateway and proxy, then review their mailbox rules
options.why: Credential reset plus session revocation cuts off the attacker; gateway blocks stop the campaign's spread.

options.text: Do nothing — the phishing page is down now
options.why: Stolen credentials remain valid until reset, regardless of the page status.

options.text: Disable email for the entire company for a week
options.why: Disproportionate response that punishes everyone instead of containing the two accounts.

options.text: Ask the users to be more careful next time
options.why: Advice without technical containment leaves active compromise in place.

steps.prompt: What is the durable, long-term fix that reduces repeat clicks?

options.text: A one-time all-hands warning email
options.why: One-off warnings fade within days and build no skill.

options.text: Punish the two users publicly as an example
options.why: Punishment drives under-reporting; you want more reports, not fewer.

options.text: Recurring phishing simulations, short role-based training, and a one-click report-phish button in the mail client
options.why: Measured simulations plus frictionless reporting convert users from targets into detectors.

options.text: Block all external email attachments permanently
options.why: Over-blocking breaks legitimate business while attackers pivot to links and QR codes.

scenarios.title: Cloud Misconfiguration Audit
scenarios.context: A routine review finds an object-storage bucket with public-read ACLs holding customer PII, an IAM user with AdministratorAccess whose access key is three years old, and no centralized logging on the account.

steps.prompt: Immediate action on the public bucket holding PII?

options.text: Leave it — nobody has complained
options.why: Public PII exposure is an active breach risk regardless of complaints.

options.text: Enable block-public-access and remove the public ACL/policy, then verify with an external check
options.why: Removing public access first stops the bleeding; verification confirms the fix.

options.text: Delete the bucket and its contents immediately
options.why: Deletion destroys data the business needs and any forensic trail of who accessed it.

options.text: Rename the bucket so attackers cannot find it
options.why: Security by obscurity — the bucket remains publicly readable under a new name.

steps.prompt: How do you remediate the over-privileged IAM user with the ancient key?

options.text: Rotate the access key and scope the user down to least-privilege permissions for their actual job
options.why: Key rotation kills stale credentials; least privilege shrinks what a compromise can do.

options.text: Share the existing key with the team to avoid lockouts
options.why: Sharing multiplies the exposure of an already stale credential.

options.text: Do nothing — the user needs admin 'just in case'
options.why: Standing admin with a 3-year-old key is exactly the standing risk to eliminate.

options.text: Delete the user without checking what breaks
options.why: Blind deletion can break production jobs; scope down deliberately instead.

steps.prompt: What prevents the next misconfiguration from reaching production?

options.text: Hope the team remembers this incident
options.why: Memory is not a control.

options.text: Add preventive guardrails: config rules that flag public buckets, and policies that deny public storage and wildcard admin grants
options.why: Detective plus preventive guardrails make the safe configuration the default.

options.text: Ban the cloud and move everything back on-prem
options.why: A platform change does not fix a governance gap — and is rarely feasible.

options.text: Require a manager's email approval for every change
options.why: Manual approvals do not scale and are routinely rubber-stamped.

steps.prompt: How do you verify the audit is complete?

options.text: Re-scan the environment with a CSPM/misconfiguration scanner, review centralized logs, and document findings and fixes
options.why: Independent re-scanning plus log review provides evidence the issues are closed.

options.text: Ask the engineer who made the bucket if it looks fixed
options.why: Self-attestation without verification is not an audit.

options.text: Close the ticket — the immediate issues are handled
options.why: Closing without verification leaves unknown residual exposure.

options.text: Wait for the next audit cycle in a year
options.why: A year of unverified exposure is an unacceptable verification plan.

scenarios.title: Pentest Scoping & Rules of Engagement
scenarios.context: Your company hired a firm to test the customer portal. The draft contract lists 'all company systems' as in scope, with no testing windows, no forbidden actions, and only a verbal go-ahead from a project manager.

steps.prompt: How do you fix the scope before testing begins?

options.text: Accept 'all company systems' — broader is better
options.why: Undefined scope risks production outages, legal exposure, and testing systems you have no right to test.

options.text: Define explicit in-scope hosts, IPs, URLs, and APIs in writing, plus explicit out-of-scope systems (e.g., production databases, third-party SaaS)
options.why: Written scope boundaries protect both sides and keep testing legal and safe.

options.text: Let the testers decide scope as they go
options.why: Tester-defined scope is not authorization; you remain liable for what they touch.

options.text: Limit scope to the login page only
options.why: An artificially tiny scope wastes the engagement and misses real attack surface.

steps.prompt: What authorization is required for the engagement to be legal?

options.text: A verbal OK from the project manager
options.why: Verbal approval from a non-executive does not constitute legal authorization to attack systems.

options.text: No authorization needed — it is our own company
options.why: Unauthorized testing can still violate contracts, regulations, and provider terms.

options.text: A signed authorization letter from an executive with authority over the in-scope systems
options.why: Written executive authorization is the legal foundation of the test — get it before any packets fly.

options.text: An email from the help desk saying 'go ahead'
options.why: The help desk cannot authorize offensive security activity.

steps.prompt: Which rules of engagement belong in the contract?

options.text: Testers may run destructive DoS attacks at any time
options.why: Unrestricted destructive testing can take down production and customers.

options.text: Defined testing windows, forbidden actions (no DoS, no data destruction/exfiltration without written approval), and emergency contacts with a kill-switch procedure
options.why: Windows, prohibitions, and an abort path keep the test controlled and recoverable.

options.text: No rules — real attackers do not follow rules
options.why: You are hiring professionals, not simulating chaos; uncontrolled testing is negligence.

options.text: Testers must never communicate until the final report
options.why: Silence removes your ability to stop a test that is causing harm.

trainers.title: Well-Known Port Trainer
trainers.brief: Rapid-fire numeric recall of the TCP/UDP ports every defender must know cold: 22 SSH, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 110 POP3, 143 IMAP, 443 HTTPS, 445 SMB, 1433 MSSQL, 3306 MySQL, 3389 RDP, 5432 PostgreSQL, 5900 VNC, 8080 HTTP-alt. Timed rounds with instant correction.

trainers.title: CIA-Triad Scenario Trainer
trainers.brief: Scenario prompts describe a security event or control (ransomware encrypting files, a checksum mismatch, a DDoS taking down a site) and you classify which leg of the CIA triad is threatened or protected — confidentiality, integrity, or availability — with an explanation of why.

mockTasks.q: Risk is best described as:
choices: A function of threat, vulnerability, and impact
mockTasks.explain: Risk models the potential for loss as threat x vulnerability x impact. (Module 1)

mockTasks.q: TCP operates at which layer of the OSI model?
mockTasks.explain: TCP is a Layer 4 (Transport) protocol providing reliable delivery; IP is Layer 3. (Module 2)

mockTasks.q: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 organizes outcomes into which Functions?
choices: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
Plan, Do, Check, Act, Review, Audit
mockTasks.explain: CSF 2.0 has six Functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. (Module 3)

mockTasks.q: An exploit is:
choices: Code or a technique that takes advantage of a vulnerability
mockTasks.explain: Vulnerability = weakness; exploit = the thing that leverages it; payload = what runs after. (Module 4)

mockTasks.q: CISA recognizes how many critical infrastructure sectors?
mockTasks.explain: CISA designates 16 critical infrastructure sectors, from Energy to Healthcare. (Module 5)

mockTasks.q: Multi-factor authentication requires:
choices: A password plus a password hint
Two or more independent authentication factors of different types
mockTasks.explain: MFA combines distinct factor types (knowledge, possession, inherence) so one stolen factor is not enough. (Module 6)

mockTasks.q: What distinguishes an IPS from an IDS?
choices: An IPS sits inline and can block malicious traffic; an IDS only detects and alerts
An IDS blocks traffic and an IPS only watches
An IPS works only on encrypted traffic
mockTasks.explain: IDS = detection (alerts); IPS = prevention (inline, can drop). Placement determines the difference. (Module 7)

mockTasks.q: Asymmetric cryptography uses:
choices: The same key on both sides
A mathematically related public/private key pair
mockTasks.explain: Public key encrypts/verifies, private key decrypts/signs. Symmetric crypto uses one shared key. (Module 8)

mockTasks.q: The primary role of a SOC Tier 1 analyst is:
choices: Initial alert triage, enrichment, and escalation
mockTasks.explain: Tier 1 triages the alert queue; Tier 2 investigates; Tier 3 hunts and engineers detections. (Module 9)

mockTasks.q: NIST SP 800-61 orders incident response phases as:
choices: Preparation; Detection & Analysis; Containment, Eradication & Recovery; Post-Incident Activity
mockTasks.explain: SP 800-61 lifecycle: prepare, detect/analyze, contain/eradicate/recover, then post-incident lessons learned. (Module 10)

mockTasks.q: Hardening a server most directly means:
choices: Reducing its attack surface by disabling unneeded services and accounts
Giving all users sudo for convenience
Turning off logging to improve performance
mockTasks.explain: Hardening = minimize what is exposed: fewer services, fewer accounts, secure defaults. (Module 11)

mockTasks.q: Under the cloud shared responsibility model:
choices: The provider secures the cloud itself; the customer secures what they put in the cloud
mockTasks.explain: Provider owns physical hosts/hypervisor; you own your data, identities, and configurations. (Module 12)

mockTasks.q: In a black-box penetration test, the tester:
choices: Has full source code and credentials
Has no prior knowledge of the target
Works only from inside the network
mockTasks.explain: Black box = zero prior knowledge (external attacker view); white box = full knowledge; gray box = partial. (Module 13)

mockTasks.q: A professional penetration test report must include:
choices: Findings with severity ratings, evidence, and remediation guidance
Only the list of tools used
A guarantee the client is now secure
The testers' personal opinions of the staff
mockTasks.explain: Reports need an executive summary plus technical findings: severity, evidence, impact, remediation. (Module 14)

mockTasks.q: Pretexting is:
choices: A social engineering attack using a fabricated scenario to extract information
mockTasks.explain: Pretexting invents a believable pretext (e.g., 'IT support') to manipulate the target. (Module 15)

mockTasks.q: Prompt injection is an attack primarily targeting:
mockTasks.explain: Prompt injection crafts inputs that make an AI system ignore instructions or leak data. (Module 16)

mockTasks.q: Data minimization (a core privacy principle) means:
choices: Collecting as much data as possible
Collecting only the personal data needed for the stated purpose
mockTasks.explain: Collect only what you need, keep it only as long as needed — less data, less breach impact. (Module 17)

mockTasks.q: In operational technology (OT) environments, which leg of the CIA triad is typically prioritized?
mockTasks.explain: OT runs physical processes: safety and continuous availability outrank confidentiality. (Module 18)

mockTasks.q: The STRIDE threat-modeling mnemonic covers:
choices: Servers, Threats, Risks, Incidents, Defenses, Events
Scan, Target, Recon, Intrude, Destroy, Exit
Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege
Strategy, Tactics, Resources, Intel, Defense, Execution
mockTasks.explain: STRIDE maps threat categories to security properties; pair it with DREAD for scoring. (Module 19)

mockTasks.q: Defense in depth means:
choices: Layered, overlapping controls so one failure does not equal compromise
mockTasks.explain: Multiple independent layers (perimeter, endpoint, identity, data) contain failures. (Module 20)

mockTasks.q: The Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain has how many stages?
mockTasks.explain: Seven: Reconnaissance, Weaponization, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, C2, Actions on Objectives. (Module 21)

mockTasks.q: The main purpose of an incident response tabletop exercise is to:
choices: Validate IR plans and roles through guided discussion before a real incident
mockTasks.explain: Tabletops walk the team through a scenario to find plan gaps without real-world cost. (Module 22)

mockTasks.q: MTTR (Mean Time to Respond/Recover) measures:
choices: How many alerts fire per day
How long vulnerabilities exist before patching
The average time to restore service after an incident
The cost of the SOC per analyst
mockTasks.explain: MTTD = detect, MTTR = respond/recover; both are core SOC performance metrics. (Module 23)

mockTasks.q: Responsible vulnerability disclosure means:
choices: Publishing the exploit immediately for fame
Selling the bug to the highest bidder
Reporting the flaw privately to the vendor and allowing time to fix before public disclosure
mockTasks.explain: Coordinated disclosure gives the vendor a remediation window while protecting users. (Module 24)

mockTasks.q: A risk register is used to:
choices: Document identified risks, owners, likelihood, impact, and treatment plans
mockTasks.explain: The risk register is the living inventory of risks and their treatment decisions. (Module 1)

mockTasks.q: Role-based access control (RBAC) grants access based on:
choices: The user's job role and its required permissions
mockTasks.explain: RBAC maps permissions to roles, users to roles — simplifying least-privilege management. (Module 6)

mockTasks.q: TLS provides:
choices: Encrypted data in transit plus server authentication
mockTasks.explain: TLS encrypts traffic in flight and (with certificates) authenticates the server. (Module 8)

mockTasks.q: A SIEM's core value is:
choices: Centralizing logs and correlating events across sources to detect attacks
mockTasks.explain: SIEM = aggregation + correlation + alerting across the estate. (Module 7)

mockTasks.q: Chain of custody for digital evidence requires:
choices: Documenting who handled evidence, when, and what was done at every step
Keeping evidence on a sticky note
Emailing disk images to the team
mockTasks.explain: Unbroken documented custody keeps evidence admissible and trustworthy. (Module 10)

mockTasks.q: Which is a classic cloud misconfiguration?
choices: Enabling MFA on the root account
A storage bucket left publicly readable
mockTasks.explain: Public storage buckets and wildcard IAM policies are the textbook cloud exposures. (Module 12)

blocks.body: Risk is a function of threat, vulnerability, and impact. Treatment options: avoid, mitigate, transfer (insurance), or accept (with sign-off).
blocks.code: risk = threat x vulnerability x impact

blocks.body: Six outcome-driven functions: Govern (new in 2.0), Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. Map controls and gaps to these.
blocks.code: GV | ID | PR | DE | RS | RC

blocks.body: NIST CSF / RMF, ISO 27001, SOC 2, PCI DSS for card data, HIPAA for health data, CMMC for defense contractors.
blocks.code:
NIST-800-53 controls -> RMF authorize
ISO 27001 Annex A controls

blocks.body: Qualitative: high/medium/low matrices, fast. Quantitative: ALE = SLE x ARO in dollars, slower but board-friendly.
Symmetric (AES): one shared key, fast, bulk encryption. Asymmetric (RSA/ECC): key pair, key exchange and signatures.
blocks.code:
AES-256-GCM  -> bulk data
RSA-2048 / ECC P-256 -> key exchange, signatures

blocks.body: Hashes are one-way digests for integrity. Passwords need adaptive KDFs (bcrypt/argon2), never fast hashes (MD5/SHA-1).
blocks.code:
sha256sum file.iso   # integrity check
# passwords: bcrypt / argon2id with unique salt

blocks.body: Verify cert chain, expiry, and protocol version from the terminal before trusting a service.
blocks.code:
openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host < /dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates -issuer
nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 host

blocks.body: Generate with a CSPRNG, store in a KMS/HSM, rotate on schedule or compromise, never hardcode in repos.
blocks.code:
# NEVER: api_key = "sk-live-..." in git
# use: vault / KMS / env-backed secret manager

blocks.body: Drop everything inbound by default; allow loopback, established return traffic, then narrow service exceptions.
blocks.code:
iptables -P INPUT DROP
iptables -A INPUT -i lo -j ACCEPT
iptables -A INPUT -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp -s 10.0.0.0/8 --dport 22 -j ACCEPT

blocks.body: Nmap enumerates hosts/ports/services; tcpdump/tshark captures packets for protocol-level analysis.
blocks.code:
nmap -sV -O 10.0.0.0/24
sudo tcpdump -i any -n port 53
tshark -r cap.pcap -Y "dns" -T fields -e dns.qry.name | sort | uniq -c

blocks.body: IDS detects and alerts; IPS sits inline and blocks; SIEM centralizes logs and correlates across sources.
blocks.code:
snort / suricata  -> network IDS/IPS
SIEM: aggregate -> correlate -> alert -> hunt

blocks.body: VLANs/firewall zones separate user, server, OT, and DMZ traffic so one compromise cannot roam freely.
blocks.code:
internet -> DMZ -> app tier -> db tier (no direct internet)
OT network: isolated, one-way data diode where possible

blocks.body: Preparation; Detection & Analysis; Containment, Eradication & Recovery; Post-Incident Activity. Contain before you eradicate.
blocks.code: prepare -> detect -> contain -> eradicate -> recover -> lessons-learned

blocks.body: Image before you touch, hash everything, document chain of custody. Order of volatility: memory first.
blocks.code:
dd if=/dev/sdX of=evidence.img bs=4M status=progress
sha256sum evidence.img > evidence.sha256

blocks.body: Recon, scanning/enumeration, exploitation, post-exploitation/pivoting, reporting. Scope and written authorization first — always.
blocks.code:
recon -> scan -> exploit -> pivot -> report
RULE 1: signed authorization before any packets

blocks.body: Passive recon first (DNS, certs), then careful active enumeration inside the agreed scope and window.
blocks.code:
nmap -sS -sV --top-ports 1000 <in-scope-host>
dig +short target.example.com
# report: exec summary + findings (severity, evidence, remediation)

blocks.body: Risk = threat capability × vulnerability exploitability × business impact. Score each 1–5; the product prioritizes.
Risk ID · description · T/V/I scores · owner · mitigation · residual risk · review date. A register without owners is a wish list.
Translate to business: dollars, downtime, regulatory exposure. 'CVE-XXXX, CVSS 9.8' means nothing to a board; '$2M exposure, patchable in 4 hours' does.
Strategy, roles, policy, risk management — the new sixth function. Governance first.
Asset management, risk assessment, supply chain. You can't protect what you haven't inventoried.
Access control, training, data security, platform hardening.
Continuous monitoring, anomaly detection, event analysis.
Incident management, comms, mitigation → restoration, lessons learned. RS/RC close the loop.
Playbooks, roles, tools, comms lists, tested backups. IR is won before the incident.
Triage: validate, scope, classify severity. Timeline everything from the first minute.
Isolate, remove the cause, restore to known-good. Preserve evidence throughout.
Lessons learned → control gaps closed → detection improved. The report is a deliverable, not a formality.
Recon → weaponize → deliver → exploit → install → C2 → actions. Break any link; defenders map controls per phase.
14 tactics from Reconnaissance to Impact. Map detections to techniques; gaps = unmapped techniques.
Executive summary (risk language) → methodology → findings (evidence, impact, likelihood, remediation, retest) → appendices.
Timestamped, sourced, gap-marked. Every claim cited to a log. Timelines are evidence, not narrative.

answerBank.q: How do you explain cybersecurity risk to non-technical executives?
answerBank.a: Translate technical risk into business language: dollars, downtime, and reputation. Instead of 'we have unpatched CVEs,' say 'a ransomware event on this system would halt billing for an estimated 3 days, costing roughly $X per day, with a Y% likelihood this year based on industry data.' Present 2-3 treatment options with costs (mitigate vs. transfer via insurance vs. accept), recommend one, and ask for a decision. Executives fund outcomes and trade-offs, not vulnerability counts.

answerBank.q: SOC analyst interview: walk me through how you triage a phishing alert.
answerBank.a: First I validate the alert: check the email headers (SPF/DKIM/DMARC), extract URLs and attachments, and detonate them in a sandbox rather than clicking. Then I scope: who else received it, did anyone click or enter credentials, and are there related IOCs in proxy/firewall logs. Containment follows: block IOCs at the gateway, force password resets and revoke sessions for clickers, and search for mailbox rules the attacker may have set. Finally I document the timeline and, if it is a true positive, escalate per the IR playbook and feed the IOCs back into detections.

answerBank.q: What belongs in a penetration test report?
answerBank.a: An executive summary written for leadership (business risk, no jargon), followed by methodology and scope (what was tested, what was excluded, testing windows). Then findings, each with a severity rating, clear evidence (screenshots, requests), business impact, and step-by-step remediation guidance with retest instructions. Close with a positive-findings section and strategic recommendations. The report must be reproducible: another tester should be able to follow your steps and reach the same result.

answerBank.q: Cloud security interview: how do you secure an AWS-style account?
answerBank.a: Start with identity: MFA on root, no long-lived root keys, IAM users replaced by roles with least privilege, and SCPs blocking dangerous actions. Then lock down the network and data: no public storage buckets, encryption at rest via KMS, security groups default-deny. Enable centralized logging (CloudTrail-style audit trails) shipped to an immutable bucket with alerting on anomalies. Finally add guardrails: config rules that flag drift, automated remediation for known-bad states, and regular access reviews. Misconfiguration, not exotic exploits, causes most cloud breaches.

answerBank.q: During incident response, why do you contain before you eradicate?
answerBank.a: Eradicating first — wiping malware or reimaging — without containment lets the attacker re-enter through the same unclosed path, and destroys evidence of how they got in. Containment (isolating hosts, blocking C2, disabling compromised accounts) freezes the adversary's movement while preserving forensic artifacts. Only once the scope is known and entry points are closed do you eradicate (remove malware, patch the vector) and then recover systems in priority order, verifying each is clean before it rejoins the network.

answerBank.q: Why shouldn't developers invent their own encryption, and how should passwords be stored?
answerBank.a: Custom cryptography fails because subtle flaws in key generation, padding, randomness, or protocol design are invisible to non-specialists but obvious to attackers — use vetted primitives (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) and vetted libraries. For passwords, never store plaintext or fast hashes like MD5/SHA-256: use an adaptive, salted password-hashing function such as bcrypt or Argon2id, which are deliberately slow and memory-hard so offline brute force is expensive. Each password gets a unique random salt, and work factors rise as hardware improves.

sourceLinks.name: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF)
sourceLinks.note: NIST's voluntary framework of cybersecurity outcomes: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover — the backbone of Modules 1-3 governance content.

sourceLinks.name: CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency)
sourceLinks.note: US agency guidance on critical infrastructure sectors, alerts, and incident response resources referenced across Modules 5 and 10.

sourceLinks.name: OWASP
sourceLinks.note: Open web application security community; Top 10 and testing guides underpin the offensive-security and pentesting modules.

sourceLinks.name: MITRE ATT&CK
sourceLinks.note: Knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques used for threat modeling, detection mapping, and SOC content.

sourceLinks.name: NIST SP 800-61 Computer Security Incident Handling Guide
sourceLinks.note: The incident response lifecycle (Preparation; Detection & Analysis; Containment, Eradication & Recovery; Post-Incident Activity) taught in Module 10.

sourceLinks.name: SANS Institute
sourceLinks.note: Security training and research organization; cheat sheets and whitepapers inform defensive-operations and forensics study.

sourceLinks.name: FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams)
sourceLinks.note: Global incident response community; CVSS scoring and coordinated vulnerability disclosure standards referenced in IR modules.

sourceLinks.name: Krebs on Security
sourceLinks.note: Investigative reporting on breaches, ransomware, and cybercrime — real-world case studies for threat and IR discussions.

sourceLinks.name: NIST Privacy Framework
sourceLinks.note: Voluntary privacy risk-management tool complementing the CSF; core reference for the policy, privacy, and governance module.

sourceLinks.name: NIST SP 800-40r4 — Patch Management
sourceLinks.note: Enterprise patching guidance for the vulnerability-management domain.

sourceLinks.name: NIST SP 800-53r5 — Security Controls
sourceLinks.note: The control catalog behind risk and architecture work.

sourceLinks.name: CWE Database
sourceLinks.note: Weakness enumeration for the threat/vulnerability analysis.

glossary.definition: Threat × vulnerability × impact: the prioritization product of security work.
An actor or event capable of causing harm (capability + intent).
A weakness that a threat can exploit.
Business consequence if exploited: dollars, downtime, regulatory, reputational.
The tracked list of risks with scores, owners, mitigations, and review dates.
Cybersecurity Framework: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
Layered controls across network, endpoint, identity, and data — no single point of failure.
The seven-phase attack progression; defenders break links per phase.
Adversary tactics/techniques knowledge base for detection mapping.
Computer Security Incident Handling Guide: the IR lifecycle standard.
Common Vulnerability Scoring System: severity scoring — input to prioritization, not the decision itself.
Operational Technology / Internet of Things: cyber-physical systems with safety consequences.
Controls on AI systems: input validation, output review, access limits, monitoring.
Post-incident analysis converting experience into control and detection improvements.

faq.q: What jobs does this certificate prepare me for?
faq.a: Analyst-track roles: SOC analyst, risk analyst, security generalist. The deliverables (risk registers, pentest reports, IR timelines) are portfolio artifacts hiring managers recognize. Note the course's honesty framing: it prepares you independently; it confers no vendor certification.

faq.q: How is this different from IL-06?
faq.a: IL-06 is the operator track (pentest, SOC, KQL, SC-200). IL-25 is the professional-certificate track: risk, frameworks (CSF), IR lifecycle, ATT&CK analysis, and the deliverables portfolio. IL-06 teaches the hands; IL-25 teaches the practice.

faq.q: Do I need to memorize all of NIST CSF?
faq.a: Know the six functions cold and the category structure; look up subcategories. Interviews test whether you can *map* a control to the framework, not recite IDs.
The pentest report's executive summary — translating technical findings into business risk without losing accuracy. The course's report module drills this translation.

faq.q: Cloud, OT/IoT, AI — why in one course?
faq.a: Because modern estates are all three at once, and each breaks naive assumptions (cloud: shared responsibility; OT: safety > uptime; AI: novel attack surface). The evaluation module teaches the misconfiguration patterns per domain.

tips: Follow the guided path in order — each module unlocks the next. The sequence is the curriculum; skipping ahead breaks the chain.

This course maps to CompTIA Security+ (SY0-701) and CompTIA CySA+ (CS0-003) (independent preparation — no affiliation). Weight your drill time toward the heaviest exam domains shown in the cert gates.

The math modules (Cryptography, Prereq Math: Number Theory for Cybersecurity Professional, Prereq Math: Statistics & Probability for Cybersecurity Professional) are load-bearing — finish them before the applied modules that assume them.
Quiz-gated modules need 70%+ to unlock the next. When you miss a question, ask Noah to walk you through the miss Socratically before re-attempting.
Do each hands-on lab twice — once following the guide, once from a blank screen. The second pass is where the skill sticks.
This is a 111-hour course: at 10 focused hours a week it takes about 3 months. Short daily sessions beat weekend cramming — pace it like a semester.
